en: Salutation to the venerable Brahmā.
Salutation to that venerable Guru, by whom the eye was opened for one blinded by the darkness of ignorance, using the ointment-stick of knowledge. (1)
O Protector, O Supreme Lord, that which was explained by you at the beginning in many ways through various scriptures and illusions, along with the disciples of the Sage; || 2 ||
O God of gods, you who destroy the suffering of existence, our minds have been bewildered by listening to many scriptures. (3)
By what cause is my karma produced, and what indeed is that yoga said to be?
Yoga is declared to be sixfold, and its diversity is observed.
O Lord, tell me with certainty: how can there be a connection between this scripture—which is divided by internal distinctions—and the many other scriptures enjoined by various systems? (5)
Having heard of the supreme devotion of the gods, the sage [asked]: "By what path do those terrible dwellings in the womb not exist? || 6 ||
The Blessed Viṣṇu spoke that which is approved by all: "Indeed, you have related that secret, the most excellent mystery. (7)
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
This is the ritual manual of the Akula tradition; listen, for I shall speak it.
Within the Vedic scriptures, however, the yoga of one's own [inner] support is praised.
By that very same manifold division, all [beings] have been deluded;
yet in all the scriptures, the sages have established the equilibrium of Yoga.
O Janārdana, where and for whom was that scripture proclaimed by Śambhu?
[It was] on the beautiful peak of the Himālaya mountain, variegated with various minerals.
It was crowded with many trees, beautified by enclosures of flowers,
and frequented by all the sacred fords, including the Gaṅgā and other rivers.
In a meritorious place, most serene, auspicious, and free from disturbances;
in a solitary, secluded, and hidden spot that brings delight to the mind. || 12 ||
In that center was Mahādeva, the supreme deity of the gods,
who, having become equipoised in the Siddhāsana, was fully perfected in yogic practices.
Established in meditation, that Śiva, the Supreme Lord, reflected upon that which is stainless, formless, free from conceptual construction, and incomparable.
The Supreme Brahman was complete, and Maheśvara was absorbed within it;
at one time, Mahāmāyā, the consort of Śambhu, arrived there.
O Pārvatī, having seen Hara established in samādhi, offer him praise.
The Goddess said:
Salutations to you, the Primordial Lord; salutations to you, the Lord of the Universe. || 16 ||
Salutations to You who possess the universal form; salutations to You who transcend the universe.
Salutations to You who are the root of the universe; salutations to You who are the seed of the universe. 17.
Salutations to You who abide both outside and within; salutations to the Sustainer of the Universe.
O Supreme Lord, You are the cause of creation, maintenance, and destruction.
Even you, divided threefold, appear in the forms of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva;
salutations to you whose nature is Rajas, and salutations to you whose nature is Sattva.
Obeisance to you whose form is darkness; salutations again and again to you who are beyond the qualities (nirguṇa).
You are the science of the supreme self (adhyātmavidyā) among all sciences, O Lord of the Gods.
May he protect; through knowledge, the perfected ones attain supreme bliss.
Obeisance to you, Jātavedas, whose true nature is like the moon and other luminaries. 21.
Salutations to the one whose nature is prāṇa and apāna, who is the essence of the Śabdabrahman;
to the one who is the threefold Veda, the drinker of Soma, the bestower of fruits, and the embodiment of the qualities.
Salutations to you, Mahādeva, who exists as ignorance;
you are Gāyatrī, Sāvitrī, Mahāmāyā, and Sarasvatī. (23)
Salutations to you who are the three junctions of time, the three periods, and whose body is the triple Veda of all goddesses;
salutations to you who are the three voids and the five vital breaths.
O Lord of beings and the source of all existence, salutations to You who dwell within all beings!
Having become the very essence of day and night, You remain established as the wheel of Māyā.
And for the sake of the calculation of the lifespan of all beings, salutations to you who are in the form of sound; salutations to you who are in the form of the Bindu. || 26 ||
Obeisance to you, the form of Time; obeisance to you, the Great Vital Breath (mahāprāṇa). You are established everywhere indeed, through the distinctions of the gross and the subtle.
O Goddess, you are to be known through wisdom by sages of purified soul;
salutations to you, the letter 'A', and salutations again and again to you, the letter 'U'.
Salutations to you, O Makāra, whose form consists of the three *praṇavas*;
you are the self of knowledge, realization, and the secret, the immutable peak-syllable yet devoid of all peaks. || 29 ||
O Maheśvara, who is free from duality and non-duality and is accessible through meditative realization;
salutations to You, whose form is the mantra and who consists of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas. 30.
Homage again and again to the letter *Ha*, which is the seed-form of all mantras;
you are with form and yet formless, abiding within the body, beyond primordial nature (*prakṛti*).
The self-luminous Supreme Self, though one, exists in many ways. || 32 ||
Salutations to you whose form is knowledge; salutations to you, the giver of knowledge. Salutations to you, the all-knowing one; and salutations to you who pervade all.
At the end of the twenty-four principles is the Puruṣa, the twenty-fifth;
you are that living soul (jīva), dependent on the qualities (guṇas) and indeed driven by Māyā like a puppet on a string.
Salutations to you who are in the form of a swan; salutations to you, the supreme swan (parahaṃsa).
Salutations to you, the pure consciousness residing within all principles (tattvas). || 35 ||
You are the friendship of all beings and the supreme life-force of living creatures;
without you, there is no one who bestows the fruit of actions upon those who perform them.
Salutations to you who have the form of the Imperishable, to Death known as the Drink;
salutations to you, the Imperishable, the destroyer of untimely death.
O God, you are the supreme sacred ford among all sacred fords, the great vow among all vows, and the greatest purifier among all sacrifices. (38)
You are the mind, you are the form of the vital breath, you are the knower of the field (kṣetrajña), and you abide within the heart;
you are the non-doer, the indifferent one, the impeller, and the protector of dharma.

Salutations to you who are the form of sound; salutations to you who are the form of touch. Salutations to you whose nature is taste and whose nature is form; salutations to you who possess the form of fragrance.
For while there is perishability in another body, even in the external [world], he is of an imperishable nature;
the Supreme Person is indeed distinct, the Supreme Self, the Lord of the universe. (41)
O Śambhu, whose body consists of the principles (tattvas), salutations to you who are the self of the five elements—earth, water, fire, air, and space. 42.
Salutations to that Kapardin, who in each age is the Dharma— whether one-footed, two-footed, three-footed, or indeed four-footed.
Salutations to you who are the form of primordial nature (prakṛti) and the form of the person (puruṣa);
salutations to you whose very essence is both duality and non-duality, and who are devoid of all division.
You are formless, you are infinite, and by your own māyā you possess form;
you are the creator, the destroyer, the Lord, the witness, the sustainer, the non-enjoyer, and the Great Sovereign.
O Virūpākṣa, homage be to you; O Nīlagrīva, homage to you!
O Gaṅgādhara, homage to you; homage to you, the moon-crested one! || 46 ||
Indra and the other guardians of the world, the yakṣas, gandharvas, and kinnaras, as well as the siddhas, vidyādharas, and all other deities who are your lords; || 47 ||
Salutations to you whose form is awakening; salutations to you who are both the awakener and that which is to be awakened.
Salutations to the awakener of the universe; salutations to you who are the awakening of primordial knowledge. 48.
This entire universe, both stationary and moving, consisting of the mobile and the immobile, is enveloped by karma; O Supreme Lord, you are its protector. 49.
You are the teacher of all sentient beings, the instructor residing within the heart;
O Lord, through the practice of yoga and the instruction on existence and karma, you bestow liberation. (50)
O Great Lord, you are indeed inconceivable, immeasurable, and imperishable;
you are the support of all, yourself without support, the architect of the worlds.

O God, you are the refuge of those seeking refuge, the destroyer of sins, and the source of compassion; [save] us who have come for protection, agitated by the waves of worldly existence and drenched in blood and flesh. (52)
O Lord, you who grant compassion and bring fearlessness to your devotees,
you who are the destroyer of the suffering of the afflicted— look upon us with your compassionate gaze.
Having recognized You as the Lord of the entire universe, the source of all seeds,
and that which is beyond both Śakti and Śiva— the eternal, infinite Brahman.
Thus entreated by Pārvatī in various ways,
Maheśvara’s mind ceased from meditation and he became moved by her praise.
At that moment, the goddess Śāmbhavī-kalā, filled with joy,
bowed to Mahādeva and asked this question.
Therefore, O Śiva, best of gods, please out of compassion accept my words:
I have heard in the scriptures that there are infinite paths distinguished by their respective actions.
My mind has been deluded by them; I do not remember what is true.
Therefore, O Omniscient One, tell me the reason for the Vedas and the Śāstras. (58)

There is a divergence among all the scriptures, yet there is also a single unified intent; while there is dispute within the six systems of philosophy, the underlying inquiry remains established in the mind.
Is liberation attained through action alone, or by means of yoga and its practice?
Yoga is declared to be one in all the scriptures; why then is it described in many ways?
O ascetic, what are the six limbs of yoga?
O Mahādeva, explain this other question to me according to its true meaning. (61)
Who is the individual soul (jīva) residing in all beings, and what is the power consisting of the qualities (guṇas)?
And who, O Lord, is the Supreme Self (paramātman) devoid of qualities, yet the witness of the individual soul? (62)
By what means does the union with Brahman arise for the individual soul that is bound by sin and merit and has fallen into the ocean of worldly existence? (63)
O Lord of the Gods, by what means may there be the stabilization of these two: a body marked by wrinkles and grey hair, and men who are devoted to knowledge? (64)
Having heard these words, Śiva, the lord of Kailāsa,
looked upon Pārvatī with compassion through his two eyes and spoke to her.
The illustrious Lord said:

Through the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas, and by means of all the various scriptures, manifold distinctions have been fashioned for the purpose of creation; yet in the ultimate sense, there is no distinction.
Through the path of karma, there is saṃsāra; through the path of Veda, it is certain [of liberation];
through the path of Yoga, there is mokṣa—that yoga which consists of the union of Śiva and the individual soul.
Within the inner science (adhyātmaśāstra), however, a single uniformity is observed;
there is no diversity in yoga, though one may conceive of a distinction based on names. (68)
The names of the One are manifold, divided by distinctions in many ways; indeed, through these very designations, all people speak of You, O Yogin. (69)
O beloved, even if one has studied the Vedas along with their six auxiliary limbs and the various scriptures such as the Āgamas, there is no true knowledge without a guru.
Therefore, for that man who, having carefully examined his guru, worships Śivā, they clearly impart the knowledge of Yoga; of this there is no doubt. (71)
In this worldly existence, there is no savior for living beings other than the true guru;
by destiny, the vision of him arises through the excellence of one's knowledge. (72)
I shall describe the limbs of yoga by which practitioners attain success;
O beautiful one, contemplate these twelve divisions of yoga within yourself. 73.
Posture, restraint of the breath, withdrawal of the senses, concentration, meditation, and absorption—these, O one of great austerity, are the limbs of yoga. (74)

First, O auspicious lady, the divine seat (āsana) is to be meditated upon; it removes all ailments. At its entry, it is remembered as imperishable within the body during the practice of breath-filling (pūraka).
The second limb of yoga is declared to be prāṇāyāma; when performed steadily at the region of the navel, it destroys all sins. (76)

And know the third, O Lord, to be upward-moving and consisting of withdrawal (pratyāhāra), residing in the heart; it effects the piercing of the knots and so forth, destroying the objects of the mind.
In the fourth [cakra], that which is called Dhāraṇa is situated in the wheel of vowels;
it consists of nectar, is exceedingly gentle, and by means of it, poetic talent is born.
The fifth meditation is situated between the eyebrows; it is indicated by the Vedas, bestows the eight supernatural powers upon men, and is proclaimed as a limb of yoga.
The sixth indeed is the sky situated in the middle, O dear one, which is most difficult to attain;
it is renowned as Samādhi, the illuminator of all knowledge.
Therefore, the yogi is called Mahādevī and Parameśvara;
like Brahman and like Yoga, he is difficult to perceive even by the gods.
These indeed are declared to be the six limbs of yoga;
by means of these limbs, O fair-faced one, many yogins have attained perfection.
The state of Brahman is the seat (āsana), while breath control (prāṇāyāma) belongs to Viṣṇu;
withdrawal of the senses (pratyāhāra) is the state of Rudra, and concentration (dhāraṇā) is considered to reside in Īśvara.
Meditation is Sadāśiva, and the state of Samādhi belongs to Puruṣa;
having thoroughly practiced those states of being, the yogi becomes established in Brahman.
Those who possess the highest knowledge of the inner self declare that these are the six limbs, which are agreed upon by all through the half-circulation of the vital breath (prāṇa). || 85 ||
O one of great asceticism, listen with focused attention to another form of Śakti, which is the very nature of the individual soul—the all-pervading Brahman. (86)
Abiding within the three channels according to the division of the three qualities,
that [consciousness] situated in the heart and joined with activity is called the "living being" (jīva) by the wise.
Being immovable and of pure being, one is liberated through that knowledge. || 93 ||
The severing of the bonds will surely occur through the union of mind and vital breath;
yet the conjunction of mind and vital breath does not indeed happen without the *praṇava*. 94.
O lady of excellent countenance, through the practice of the *praṇava*, the yogi becomes equal to me;
the *praṇava* is declared by the virtuous to consist of three breath-controls (*prāṇāyāma*).
O Śiva, the lowest, the middling, and the highest [levels] have been proclaimed;
the yogi should practice gradually, following the sequence beginning with the postures (āsana). 96.
Having abandoned sleep, moderate in diet, having mastered his breath and conquered his senses, the yogi who is constantly devoted to the practice of yoga becomes equal to Brahman. 97.
O Pārvatī, through the practice of yoga, the individual soul attains union with Śiva;
having abandoned the left and right [channels], one should practice at the root of the vital breath.
Through practice, the knot of the heart is gradually severed;
by the movement within the internal channels, the individual soul becomes one with Śiva. 99.
Though possessed of qualities, he is proclaimed as one who has transcended qualities and is the cutter of bonds;
the severing of bonds must be accomplished through the singular yoga of breath control (prāṇāyāma).
The union of prāṇa and apāna and the purification of the channels are attained;
having correctly understood the method of yoga, one should practice the unification of the two. (101)
Endowed with that practice, O Dear One, he becomes your practitioner;
for him there shall be no death, and he will be free from old age and grey hair.
The skin-fold (valī) is renowned as the primordial nature (prakṛti), and the gray hair (palita) is remembered as the person (puruṣa);
these two states are established within the two elements through their gross, subtle, and other modes of being. 103.
O beloved, when they delight in passion (raja), they are named Sūrya and Candramas;
when that state of equilibrium occurs in the void, it is called "stambhana" (the arresting).
The knowledge of wrinkles and grey hair, as well as their immobilization, is proclaimed;
the rejuvenation of the body beyond a hundred years is also declared. (105)
The man who knows yoga is born endowed with all auspicious marks;
as long as the aging of the body is seen, it is turned back. (106)
Again and again, without a doubt, until the limit of a hundred [years];
through practice for a hundred years, old age is cast off once more.
Having conquered death, the yogi may then wander upon the earth free from fear;
for as long as the body has not yet perished, the yogi’s practice does not cease.
O observer of noble vows, as long as the stainless self, known as the individual soul (jīva), is not stable,
it will become stable through practice performed over a long period of time.
Accompanied by all virtues and manifesting through various signs, there is thereafter no pain in the body, nor does old age exist at all. (110)
A living being may appear with a beautiful body or a deformed one;
since its majesty is inconceivable, you should not therefore hold anyone in contempt. (111)

One who lacks faith, whose nature is evil, an atheist, one whose doubts are shattered [by false reasoning], a mere logician, and one who acts like a heron— these are not within the sphere of the wise.
Those fools who do not know the divine play of that Lord of Yogins and instead utter insults—being the most sinful—they will certainly fall into hell. (113)
One should never entertain doubt regarding the body of any yogin;
for they sport in the three worlds just like ordinary people. 114.
O Pārvatī, those who utter insults against the Lord of Yoga, the Yogin, and the science of Yoga, are therefore designated as Rākṣasas.
Those who are heretics, devoted to sin, and averse to their own dharma—for them, the yogi who has been insulted shall not be a protector on this earth. (116)
O lady of virtuous vows, the life-span, beauty, fame, and merit of that person perish, whose mind, through the practice of yoga, becomes clouded by delusion. (117)
For one to whom dharma is repugnant, yoga does not take root;
he too experiences the suffering of birth from a womb continuously. || 118 ||
O beloved, according to the karma of each individual, such is their inclination; the disposition of living beings arises based upon their merit and demerit. (119)
Through the conjunction of the nature of wind, that which has been and that which is to be are established;
this is proclaimed in the Nāmaveda through the union of mind and vital breath.
O Mountain-Self, those who do not know the unity of these two— the Sāṃkhya and Yoga, which are the mind and the vital breath within this body— undergo birth again and again.
As long as there is the activity of the mind there, so long is there the activity of the wind; and as long as there is the activity of the wind, so long is there the activity of the mind.
There, from the destruction of one comes the destruction of the other, and from the activity of one comes the activity of the other. (122)

Even for one whose group of sense faculties is pure and whose attainment of the state of liberation is destroyed, the cessation of the vital breath can still be accomplished by one who is devoted to the six-limbed yoga. 123.
That which is indeed the mind is the vital breath (prāṇa), and that which is the vital breath is known as the mind;
it exists in all living beings in the form of the perishable and the imperishable.
Liberation occurs through the equality of mind and vital breath, and not otherwise.
This has been declared as the most profound secret; it must not be given to just anyone. 125.
[Thus ends the first chapter in the glorious Akulāgama-mahātantra, the Yogasārasamuccaya. || 1 ||
The Goddess said:
Today my birth has become fruitful; today my austerity has become fruitful;
today my knowledge has become fruitful through your grace, O ender of worldly existence.
O Maheśvara, you have declared in all the scriptures that there are two types—action and non-action;
yet I have no discernment regarding them, and thus doubt remains within me.
What is to be known as improper action? The auspicious and inauspicious nature of bulbs and roots;
the four states of mind; and the discernment of dharma and adharma. (3)
O Lord, what is the nature of the bondage of saṃsāra, and what is the characteristic of liberation?
What indeed is death, as well as existence and non-existence? (4)
Laya, Haṭha, Mantrayoga, and Rājayoga, O Śaṅkara;
and Sahaja according to my knowledge—I shall describe them to you, O Lord of the Gods. (5)
The illustrious Lord said:
"O Goddess, you have composed this *Praśnasamuccaya*, the essence of the Vedas;
I shall explain it to you in due order, so listen and hold it in your heart."
"What is action? What is inaction? Even the wise are bewildered by this.
Therefore, I shall declare to you that action, by knowing which you will be liberated from evil. (7)
For one must understand action, and what is to be understood regarding improper action; one must also understand inaction, and the subtle course of non-action. (8)

One should understand that which decays as action (karma) and that which is designated as the imperishable (akṣara) as non-action (akarma); one who is liberated from both the perishable and the imperishable attains the state beyond action (vikarma).
It is perfected by the essence of non-action, equal and characterized by fire;
it is designated as the moon of action and is firmly established in the vital breath.
The apāna wind always abides in the form of the sun of non-action;
these varieties have been fully described as arising from action, non-action, and mis-action.
He who sees action in inaction and inaction in action is wise among men; he is disciplined and a performer of all actions.
To him whose nature is Bindu and Nāda, in whom karma and akarma exist in two ways;
now I shall describe the Kanda, which is indeed the root and the cause of all. (13)
The yogi who practices equanimity is disciplined and a performer of all actions;
this investigation into action and inaction has been declared as truly secret. (14)
In the center of the navel resides the Great Goddess; there stands the kanda, whose nature is Śiva, where the oblation of moon and sun is consecrated by the mantra "Śakti Svāhā."
It has the appearance of the fire of cosmic destruction, it is throbbing, and it is the abode of Śiva;
it is endowed with the ten elements and devoid of the five subtle elements.
I consider that very life-force, which by its own nature presides over the world of living beings, to be dead without *niyati*, even though it resides within the body like a bulbous root. (17)
That whirlwind of the wind is also declared to be the Mantra-pīṭha;
its Vidyā-pīṭha consists of the mudrās and the maṇḍala itself.
It is the root of all the cakras and the planets, just as the sun is [the source] of all;
this is the kanda-root, O blessed lady—now hear concerning the auspicious and the inauspicious.
The auspicious is declared to be the doctrine of Śiva; the inauspicious is the doctrine of Prakṛti.
Know that which is both auspicious and more than auspicious to be the eternal doctrine of Brahman.
Four states of the mind are to be known within the body:
waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and the fourth state (turya), distinguished by their different conditions. || 21 ||
The first stage is in the heart; the second goes to the end of the sixteen [fingers];
the third is in the middle of the palate; and the fourth is in the aperture of space (the crown of the head). // 22 //
O Dear One, all these modifications consisting of the mind, which reside within bodies, are to be known as being struck by the Suṣumnā within the Praṇava. 23.
I have described the fourfold state of mind as being of two kinds;
first, I shall explain the characteristics of dharma and adharma.
Know that both dharma and adharma are my two embodied portions;
they consist of the nature of Agni and Soma, and have the form of day and night. (25)
The white and black [paths] are proclaimed as being designated by truth and falsehood;
they are to be known as the sun and the moon, the stable and the unstable, the supreme and the lower. (26)
Renowned as Heaven and Earth, the existent and the non-existent, the imperishable and the perishable—the two birds, free from passion and devoid of impurity—are recited in the Vedic scriptures. (27)
Difference and non-difference, liberation and bondage, as well as the conscious and the unconscious, are described;
likewise, the two known by the names Iḍā and Piṅgalā are called the Jāhnavī and the Yamunā. (28)
But what is the use of much speaking, O beloved? Knowledge and ignorance are of various kinds and names, established as dharma and adharma. (29)
Dharma is characterized by the notion of "above," while adharma is characterized by the notion of "below";
but the Supreme Brahman is beyond all notions, whereas the individual soul (jīva) has the nature of the movement of conceptualization.
The two paths of Bindu and Nāda have the natures of rajas and tamas respectively;
Hari and Hara are each established in both [paths] throughout the entire body. (31)
Both dharma and adharma are mixed together in the middle, consisting of action;
through them, one shall attain a self within a body defiled by passion and the like. || 32 ||
But he who restrains himself and perceives the self as eternally blissful, stainless, the witness, and the eternal, he indeed speaks of the Supreme. (33)
For in this scripture, the union of both existence and non-existence is established.
Now I shall speak of another, supreme [state]; listen to this third distinction. (34)

The aggregate known as the *liṅga*, consisting of three qualities (*triguṇa*), should be understood as having the nature of female, male, and neuter; it is characterized by *tamas*, *sattva*, and *rajas*. (35)
The first is possessed of form and eternal; his state as an object of action consists of the *kalās*.
He alone is designated as the *jīva*, the transmigrating being, and is considered conscious. (36)
The knower of the Kṣatra perceives action as being within Time and within the Self;
though it is one, it appears manifoldly divided, established in each respective principle.
For one who is attached to the fruit [of action] is bound by the form of manifold syllables;
this bondage, consisting of merit and demerit, is proclaimed to belong to the soul (jīva). || 38 ||
For him, there is no further wandering through the cycle of rebirth in successive existences;
thus is this bondage of saṃsāra established within the Kālacakra. (39)
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the classification of liberation, which is very difficult to attain:
when the mind is free from both merit and demerit and is without support. (40)
Then, for yogins, liberation occurs in the form of nirvāṇa;
the mind is said to be life, and in the absence of mind, death is certain. (41)
Having become equalized with respect to mind and no-mind, one is said here to be liberated while living;
life and death themselves have thus been briefly described by me. (42)
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain existence and non-existence as they reside within the heart:
existence is by the mere act of entering, while departure is designated as non-existence. (43)
The intrinsic nature (svabhāva) that is free from both existence and non-existence is designated as Brahman;
existence is declared to be what is called the vital breath (prāṇa), while the fearless state is termed the path (yāna). || 44 ||
O beloved, through the union of prāṇa and apāna, they proceed upon the path of Brahman,
wherein one's own true nature is contemplated— void, free from all appearances.
The yoga of non-existence (abhāvayoga) is proclaimed as the fourth characteristic of yoga;
[the others being] layayoga, haṭhayoga, and mantrayoga as the third. || 46 ||
The fourth is indeed the Rājayoga alone;
for how can there be a unity between the two—the knower of the field (kṣetrajña) and the supreme self (paramātman)? (47)
O auspicious lady, listen to this layayoga and this haṭhayoga:
the letter *ha* is known as the sun, while the letter *ṭha* has the form of the moon.
When the moon and the sun have become equalized, it is called Haṭhayoga.
By the syllable *ma* the mind (*manas*) is expressed, and by the syllable *tra* the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is denoted. (49)
The union of mind and breath is indeed what is designated as yoga, which is mantra.
Having drawn back the movement of the apāna, the prāṇa enters the central channel.
By that [practice], Rājayoga shines in the lotus of the sky;
he who is known as Indra is the letter *sa*, and the letter *ha* is said to be the Sun. (51)
O beloved, they know that innate state of those two to be formless;
there is a distinction between them in terms of names, but in the ultimate sense, there is no difference.
By the grace of the Guru's feet, the one alone is revealed;
one should dissolve the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), which is free from all states of being, into Brahman. (53)
This is both knowledge and meditation; all other extensive treatises are merely further elaboration.
[Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Dialogue between Īśvara and Pārvatī," in the *Yogasārasamuccaya*, the great tantra of the venerable *Akulāgama*. || 2 ||
The Goddess said:
"O Lord, it is said that the Supreme Brahman, which is attainable through Yoga, is the sole goal for men who follow various paths; this statement is false. (1)
O Lord, what does the Śruti declare as the definitive conclusion when it says "not this, not this" through negation?
Pray tell me the true meaning of reality as it is established in the Vedas.
That which is seen has its perception destroyed, yet that which is unseen is devoid of existence;
by what means is that state attained which is celebrated as the supreme? (3)
There is no such thing as the meditation on the invisible; that which is visible perishes.
Since Brahman is without color and without sound, how can there be meditation for one who is bound by ritual injunctions?
O Lord, a great doubt regarding the meaning of this matter dwells within my mind.
O Śambhu, wearer of matted locks, clarify what the true meaning of the Vedic revelation is.
What is wine, sexual intercourse, meat, truth, and untruth—the supreme? And what is the falling of the drop? All that is the Grasa; who are the four stages of life (āśramas)? 6.
The illustrious Lord said:
This investigation of various paths is for the purpose of retaining the meaning of the sacred revelation; let the meditation on formlessness pass away, as I shall now speak according to the truth.
Listen and sever, in their proper order: intoxicants, sexual intercourse, and meat; truth and untruth, which are unsurpassed; the emission of the drop (bindu), and morsels of food. (8)
The two paths named Iḍā and Piṅgalā are well-adorned;
known by various names, they are constantly resorted to by yogis.
Through the practice of these two, one proceeds upon the upward path,
by which path one must go to the stainless abode of Brahmā.
O Goddess, for those who follow various paths, Yoga is praised in the Veda;
such a person does not undergo rebirth and crosses over the ocean of existence.
By asserting that there is no liberation through various types of paths, he [renders] all those of wicked conduct devoid of the definitive determination of the scriptures. (12)
The heart of the scripture is one thing, yet the discourse is otherwise, O beloved;
what is the reason, O Great Goddess, that we are deluded by the māyā of Viṣṇu? (13)
Due to the connection with diverse karmas, a diversity of intellects arises; they do not remember the supreme reality, so one should avoid attachment. 14.
Then, by means of the sentences beginning with "śruti" and so forth, [the Lord] is remembered as "not this, not that" (neti neti).
He does not determine power in the first [instance], nor does He act in the second. (15)
Brahman, whose nature consists of Śiva and Śakti, is established within the Praṇava;
yet, O Supreme Goddess, they do not know the supreme state of the Lord.
The third, however, is beyond syllables; it is the unity of those two, free from all forms.
This is the supreme reality, directly perceived by the eye of knowledge. (17)
Formlessness is attained through meditation by means of breath control (prāṇāyāma), and not otherwise;
therefore, one should practice breath control with every effort. (18)
O Goddess of the gods, meditate in this way upon the supreme, eternal, and firm union situated in the foundation, until you have reached absorption in Brahman. (19)
Those who hate liquor, sexual intercourse, and meat, O Maheśvarī, fall into the most terrible Raurava hell; of this there is no doubt.
One should know that the red is wine and the white is meat, O Mistress of the Gods;
that which is the state of being a goddess, O Great Goddess, and that which is its seed, I am that, my dear. (21)
One should recognize the lotus in the hand; one should fashion the vessel as a preta.
In its center, one should meditate upon the deity whose form is mental bliss.
Ignorance should be known as the intoxicant that causes delusion and leads one astray;
knowledge is declared to be the meat that liberates and leads toward old age [the state of liberation]. (23)
O Goddess, that which consists of both knowledge and ignorance, the third point (bindu) which is of equal form—that supreme union should be known as the source of liberation. (24)

But that which is established upon the breath of ignorance relies on the breath of true knowledge; know, O lady of excellent vows, that what is called "sexual union" and "non-sexual union" is designated as threefold.
"Those who are devoted to external intoxicants, sexual intercourse, and the eating of meat—all of them go to hell; this is my true word. (26)
The *nāda* is drawn upward by the *bindu*; that is traditionally known as the drinking of wine.
The *bindu* is wounded by the *kalā*, and therefore that indeed constitutes the eating of meat. (27)
Otherwise, those of evil conduct, most sinful, and devoid of knowledge—all of them, remembered as base, proceed by a wrong path. (28)
The yogi always eats what is not to be eaten and drinks what is not to be drunk; he constantly approaches those who should not be approached—he is a yogi, of this there is no doubt. (29)
They say that what is not to be eaten is Time, and that what is not to be drunk is the Supreme Part; he who understands that which is not to be approached as the Supreme Abode is a knower of reality.
In this way, O Great Goddess, all this should be understood in the practice of yoga:
liquor, sexual union, and meat are, in brief, of the nature of the three qualities (triguṇa). || 31 ||
The conjunction of the moon, the sun, and fire should be contemplated by those seeking liberation.
This secret has been declared by me; it must be guarded with great effort. (32)
This supreme secret seed-syllable is unsurpassed knowledge;
I shall now explain it further, along with the investigation into truth and falsehood.
Aditi is known as the essence of Prāṇa, and that Moon is remembered as being with the Sun;
likewise, Oṃkāra, Bindu-Śakti, the Witness, Puruṣa, and Hari.
Thus, Truth is known as threefold, consisting of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva;
it is remembered as having three quarters, being the three Vedas, and possessing the three qualities (guṇas).
Know that what is dissolved in the low is the middle, and what is situated in the highest is the supreme;
know that the supreme moves upward—this they declare to be the truth of Brahman.
One should speak the truth; one should speak what is pleasant; one should not speak a truth that is unpalatable; nor should one speak an untruth even if it is true—this is the eternal dharma. (37)
The single syllable "Oṃ" is proclaimed as Brahman, the Truth within the Self;
that which is otherwise is declared false, being established in perishable existence.
Prāṇa is known as truth, and untruth is its opposite;
this speech consisting of both truth and falsehood is established in prāṇa alone. (39)
Dharma increases through truth; from untruth comes the destruction of dharma.
Therefore, one should speak the truth and avoid untruth. (40)

The designation "intellect" (buddhi) is that which is perceived through speech; established in the *praṇava*, one perceives both of these. Their upward articulation is indeed the vital breath (*prāṇa*) on the middle path.
One should understand this as the truth; now hear the untruth.
Speech in the form of the second smoke is indeed known as Vaikharī. 42.
As that [sound] does not ascend, the goddess Prāṇa goes downward with face turned down;
that is declared to be the nectar (amṛta), and from it, form is established in the heart.
Truth and falsehood are proclaimed according to the distinction between correct words and corrupt words;
having abandoned that which is unsteady and false, that which is steady is called truth. (44)
Through truth one attains everything; everything is established in truth.
That truth is declared to be the *recaka* [exhalation], known as Śiva, reaching to the *dvādaśānta*. (45)
O goddess of auspicious countenance, you have asked about the falling of the bindu;
therefore, I shall describe its true nature to you in its entirety.
The Bindu is the intellect, the Bindu is Śiva, the Bindu is Viṣṇu, and the Bindu is Prajāpati;
the Bindu is the all-pervading God, the Bindu is the illuminator of the three worlds. 47.

Even though he exists as one, he abides in all threads as the very essence of the three powers; by his withdrawal (nivṛtti) the universe is sustained, but through his activity (pravṛtti), he withdraws it.
Just as the drop (bindu), having become mobile, proceeds as the mark of the qualities (guṇaliṅga), so indeed does its cycle of existence (saṃsṛti) occur, with repeated dwelling in the womb. 49.
The morsel is not measured by time; the morsel is the food of Time.
He, in the form of the *bindu* and Time, devours all that is moving and unmoving. 50.
There is no other time for living beings, nor any other protector; in life and in death alike, only one thing is praised: the single drop. 51.
The drop (bindu) situated on the downward path is said to be in a state of flux;
however, when established on the upward path, the drop remains unshaken through its cessation.
Activity and cessation, life and death are certain;
the drop moves through all of this, which is indivisible even by the gods.
When the bindu abandons the seat of fire and resorts to the seat of the sun, then the body falls; of this there is no doubt.
For the sake of protecting the body, a single drop is praised;
at that time, having dissolved from its lower part, it ascends upwards. (55)
Through the falling of the bindu, old age and death come to embodied beings;
that very breath is always meditated upon by yogis as recaka.
The *bindu* is accomplished by means of the wind (*vāyu*), and there is no other means for accomplishing the *bindu*.
When the great jewel of the *bindu* is perfected, all accomplishments (*siddhi*) arise. || 57 ||
This is declared to be the Bindu according to the division of the three qualities (guṇas);
indeed, the single Bindu is the cause of creation, maintenance, and dissolution. 58.
There is no other drop in this body; the drop is said to be consciousness.
From food the drop is produced; that drop is designated as the constituent element (dhātu). || 59 ||
Thus the knower perceives that Śiva in the form of the Bindu;
by the practice and application thereof, the knower of yoga transcends death. (60)
Death occurs through the falling of the *bindu*; life comes from the movement of the *bindu*.
Therefore, with every effort, one should personally preserve the *bindu* from its enemy. 61.
If the drop (bindu) remains stable, one's lifespan increases perpetually;
if it is unstable, [the vital energies] go to ruin, and death occurs for embodied beings.
Everything that is flickering becomes flickering, while through the steady, it becomes steady;
by abandoning fickleness and thus taking refuge in the steady, one attains stability. (63)
Then, becoming motionless, he protects his physical frame;
those who know the Vedas understand that even Time passes away as non-time.
Through the practice of breath control (pavana), the body becomes of the nature of Brahman;
and by means of the yoga of formless meditation, one becomes invisible of one's own accord. 65.
That which is known as liberation while living (jīvanmukti) is not called liberation otherwise;
that liberation which occurs when the body has departed is designated as the state of being liberated (bhāva-mukti).
All this has been fully explained by me regarding the determination of the *bindu*.
Now listen, O large-eyed one, to the fourth stage, that of the "swallowing" (*grasa*). 67.
Furthermore, eight morsels are prescribed for forest-dwellers, sixteen for householders,
and thirty-two for those who are celibate students, or as much as they desire.
In this very manner has the supreme yoga been described;
and wherever doubt exists within your heart, [that too shall be explained].
Ask questions here and there within the scripture according to your own ability. || 69 ||
[Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Meditation on the Embodied Form," in the *Śrī Akulāgama*, the Great Tantra, the Compendium of the Yogaśāstra. || 3 ||
The illustrious Goddess said:
I do not ask again and again, yet I ask again and again; otherwise, there would be no certainty. O Lord, please show compassion. (1)
Terrified by the fear of saṃsāra, protect me, protect me, O Maheśvara!
O Lord, show mercy to me, you who are the one who cuts through doubt.
O Lord of the World, the path consisting of fire and smoke has been indicated by You through the way of the Sūtras within the Vedas as the northern and southern courses. || 3 ||
What is the destination by way of the path of fire, and what is the destination by way of the path of smoke?
O Maheśvara, please make the nature of fire and smoke clear.
The cycle of the moon and sun, as well as the oblation into the fire of the vital breaths,
the equinox in the form of the sun, and that which stands in the center, liberating one from worldly existence.
O God, tell me of that which is called the Haṃsa-praṇava, by which the three worlds are pervaded;
and furthermore, if there be any other secret convention, please explain it to me.
The illustrious Lord said:
Excellent, excellent! You have asked about that which is supreme, spiritual, and established in its own nature, as it is remembered in the songs of the scriptures by the True Teacher of the World.
Fire, light, day, the bright fortnight, and the six months of the northern solstice— departing there, those people who know Brahman go to Brahman.
Smoke, night, the dark fortnight, and likewise the six-month period of the sun's southern course—
attaining these, the yogi returns from where the light of the moon prevails.
They do not know the true meaning of the Gītā scripture as it really is;
deluded by the Māyā of Viṣṇu, they are joined with destruction. (10)
The two paths consisting of fire and smoke, known as the left and the right,
are named Iḍā and Piṅgalā, and they carry the flow of prāṇa and apāna.
The *prāṇa* is established in the *iḍā*, while the *apāna* rests in the *piṅgalā*.
*Prāṇa* is designated as fire, and *apāna* is proclaimed to be smoke.
These two, though distinct from one another, function together through yoga.
Brahman is the support for the first; light is the support for the second. || 13 ||
By means of the practice of going and coming, they are situated in the north and south;
through their mutual movement and transition, the transits are established. 14.
The individual soul (jīva) situated in the left channel is praised by these names:
fire, light, day, the bright fortnight, the six months of the sun's southern course (dakṣiṇāyana), and so forth. || 15 ||
And that lunar light is situated in the center of the sun;
by means of that path, through yoga, they fall into the ocean of worldly existence.
For these two paths of the world, the bright and the dark, are considered eternal;
by one a man goes to non-return, by the other he returns again. (17)
The northern course is indeed Prāṇa, and the southern course is Apāna;
these two courses are to be known as being in the eastern and southern directions respectively. (18)
Likewise, that which is known as the other, the northern [solstice], is indeed the southern course;
for those whose minds are darkened by ignorance, transmigration there is difficult to overcome. (19)
The movement of the apāna is within the prāṇa, and the prāṇa is established within the apāna;
though one, it has become twofold, standing like a tree and its shadow.
Shade is not found without a tree, nor is a tree found without shade;
likewise, O blessed lady, the prāṇa and apāna breaths are established within the body.
Although the infinite winds within the body are capable of being endured when restrained, nevertheless, listen: both prāṇa and apāna are traditionally held to be their agents. (22)
The upward-moving breath (prāṇa) should be known as consisting of the moon, and the downward-moving breath (apāna) likewise as consisting of the sun;
from both of these arises the formation of the body, its maintenance, and its dissolution.
Through the restraint of the vital breath (prāṇa), the knot of the two—the moon and the sun—is pierced;
this individual soul (jīva) certainly attains union with the Supreme Brahman. || 24 ||
The supreme southern path, situated between the glorious moon and sun, consisting of fire and smoke, has been described along with its underlying rationale. (25)
First, listen to the Prāṇāgnihotra; I shall describe this meritorious rite, which grants freedom from rebirth, that is to be kept strictly secret, located within the center of the body. (26)
Some offer the out-breath into the in-breath, and others likewise the in-breath into the out-breath;
the movement of the out-breath and in-breath is upward for those who are devoted to the out-breath and in-breath.
Others, restricted in their food, offer the life-breaths into the life-breaths;
all these are knowers of sacrifice, and by sacrifice they destroy their impurities.
The fire is situated there in the center of the two vital breaths (prāṇa and apāna);
having offered oblations with the mantra "svāhā" uttered, it is proclaimed as sacrifice (yajña). || 29 ||

The sages declare that the Prāṇāgnihotra is the supreme purifier, by which time itself is instantly conquered; it removes disease and old age while remaining in the body, and is the very essence of liberation.
The mind, freed from both sides, becomes situated in the middle;
one should know that as the equinox, devoid of existence and non-existence. || 31 ||
The left wing is known as *svabhāva* (intrinsic nature) and the right as *abhāva* (non-existence);
by these two wings of the Supreme Lord Haṃsa, the moving and the unmoving are pervaded.
The white and black fortnights are said to be the Moon and the Sun;
these two fortnights are the movement of Saṃvarta, downward and upward, on the left and the right.
Creation belongs to one side, while the other alone withdraws it by himself;
he is the Haṃsa, the agent of creation and withdrawal, by whom the universe is protected.
That Haṃsa, which is supreme bliss, Śiva, non-dual, and imperishable, must be known through inquiry by the grace of the Guru’s feet. (35)
O Haṃsa, for this reason, time is the life-force of all embodied beings;
thus, through the application of measurement, it declares everything auspicious and inauspicious.
Instability would arise for him due to the influence of the downward vital air (apāna);
however, through the union of the two winds, the *haṃsa* attains immobility. (37)
When there is immobility, the eightfold group of powers beginning with atomization (aṇimā) arises;
one attains liberation of the body and becomes a sky-walker (khecara). || 38 ||
Stability for the *haṃsa* cannot exist without the equinox (*viṣuva*);
therefore, one should accomplish the equinox through supreme detachment (*vairāgya*). (39)
On the path consisting of fire and smoke, the light in the center is praised;
one should know it as the equinox (viṣuvant), which bestows longevity and fruit. || 40 ||
The day should be known as prāṇa, and the night indeed as apāna;
the equinox is the means, and the increase [of merit] is the goal to be accomplished by those of meritorious deeds. || 41 ||
Between the two [periods of] day and night, the digit (kalā) that moves through the Brahma[-state] is the twilight (sandhyā); for those established in Kula, it is proclaimed as the equinox (viṣuva).
O bull among sages, the supreme twilight, whose nature is knowledge, should be worshipped;
since it does not exist without the equinox (viṣuva), one should therefore take recourse to the equinox.
The equinox (viṣuva) bestows the attainment of all desires and grants the fruit of nirvāṇa; it is the equinox that grants the excellent accomplishment of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa. || 44 ||
The three channels and the triple void are declared to be the three powers;
likewise, there are the three vital breaths, the three eyes, and indeed the three minds.

The three paths, the three quarters, and the three sacred utterances (vyāhṛtis) are declared; likewise the three worlds, the three times, the three Vedas, and the three syllables of the Imperishable (akṣara). || 46 ||
Likewise, there is another triad of fires, a triad of rivers such as the Gaṅgā,
the triad of Vedas, the three worlds, and what is declared as the triad of qualities (guṇas).
The three junctions of the day, the three aims of life, the three wheels, the three seats, the three drops, the three faces, the three peaks, and the three summits. || 48 ||
The entire world, consisting of the three Vedas, exists established in a threefold state;
that triad of states and locations is called the Equinox (Viṣuvat). || 49 ||
One attains merit and knowledge through the union of Śiva and Śakti, which is equal to the Vedas at the equinox; for others, there shall be no such vision.
The merit arising from sacrifices and other such acts is a means for attaining all worldly goals;
however, the merit in the restraint of breath (prāṇāyāma) is beyond the gunas and is the cause of liberation.
This entire essence of knowledge has been told to you from every perspective; remember the equinox, the knowledge of the Praṇava, which resides within the center of the body.
Yogis constantly meditate upon the Praṇava, the saving Brahman;
through knowledge of that, perfection arises at that very moment—of this there is no doubt. (53)
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva—whatever other deities there are, such as Indra and the rest, as well as the sages. || 54 ||
Yakṣas, kinnaras, gandharvas, piśācas, uragas, and rākṣasas;
likewise, the siddhas, vidyādharas, those born from sweat, and those born from eggs. || 55 ||
The entire universe, both gross and subtle, is eternally established in the Praṇava;
yet, having abandoned the Praṇava, they worship other mantras.
For them, accomplishment does not arise even in hundreds of millions of eons;
there is no ritual action, no application of karma, and no contemplation of mantras.
Since there is nothing in this world apart from the Praṇava, one should practice the Praṇava;
it is celebrated as the "Savior" (Tāraka) through its infinite names and synonyms.
The cry of the swan is the Supreme Brahman; the Praṇava faces in every direction.
All this has been declared by me; contemplate it within your heart.
"Thus, that which is praised is unmanifest"—this is the command of the Supreme Lord.
[Thus ends the fourth chapter in the Śrī Akulāgama Mahātantra, the Yogasārasamuccaya, in the dialogue between Īśvara and Pārvatī. || 4 ||
The illustrious Lord said:
Listen to the essence of all dharma and, having heard it, let it be firmly grasped:
one should not do unto others that which is disagreeable to oneself. (1)
Various actions that are disagreeable to oneself, and all such actions toward others—indeed, others are traditionally held to be Indra and the other gods. (2)

Indeed, these qualities born of primordial nature (prakṛti) are here considered to be threefold: those characterized by darkness (tāmasa), those by passion (rājasa), and those by goodness (sāttvika). They are likewise impartial (madhyastha) in this world. || 3 ||
The Lord Jīva, though permeated by Māyā, is celebrated for his qualities;
having gone from one body to another, his consciousness remains veiled by ignorance.
Therefore, one should abandon the recurrence of attachment toward the qualities (guṇas) through the power of yoga;
when the afflictions (kleśas) in the heart come to an end, he himself becomes Śiva. || 5 ||
When the yogi, liberated from the three qualities (guṇas), abides in Śiva,
then there is indeed no birth, death, old age, grief, fear, or suffering.
At that very moment, things disagreeable to oneself perish;
that location is said to possess such qualities, and one should contemplate those qualities and actions.

Freed from the state of being a constituent of the qualities (guṇas), the individual soul (jīva) goes to the state free from affliction; in the flow of the qualities there is the bondage of existence, whereas in the flow of the absence of qualities [there is liberation].
Bondage and liberation are functions within the qualities; through their differentiation, they function respectively downward and upward during the state of affliction.
When the soul, conjoined with the qualities (guṇas), proceeds along the downward path, then that which is characterized by karma should be understood as bondage. || 10 ||
When the individual soul withdraws its qualities and proceeds upon the upward path, then liberation occurs without a doubt; indeed, there is no falling back of the body.
Having heard this, which is the very essence of the Dharma, understand it well:
Māyā, consisting of what are called Āṇava, Karma, and Māyīya, is established within Brahman as the Guṇas. (12)
Some on this earth understand this convention of the treatise;
by the grace of the Guru's feet, their success is not far off. (13)
All knowledge, which consists of the science of Brahman, is extremely difficult to attain;
O Goddess, your question has been explained, for it bestows the fruit of the supreme goal. 14.
In the Āgamas and the scriptures of Mantra, various meanings have been set forth; yet, all these statements are in perfect harmony with Brahman alone. (15)
This scripture brings about great awakening, is esteemed as the hidden Veda, consists of the nature of knowledge, removes everything [that obscures], and bestows bliss through yoga. || 16 ||
In this middle [section], O Great Goddess, I have described the single syllable according to its divisions of Brahman and through the application of its various names. (17)
Meditate with perfect stillness upon Brahman—the attributeless, changeless, and non-manifest, which is eternally arisen, blissful, and immortal. 18.
[Thus ends the fifth chapter in the Śrī Akulāgama Mahātantra, the Yogasārasamuccaya, in the dialogue between Īśvara and Pārvatī. || 5 ||
The illustrious Lord said:
The offering is Brahman, the oblation is Brahman, poured by Brahman into the fire of Brahman;
one should not depart from Brahman through concentration on the action of Brahman. (1)
Within the body of Brahmā there are three types, because they are gross, subtle, and supreme;
the gross is said to be with attributes (saguṇa), while the subtle is both with and without attributes (nirguṇa). || 2 ||
O beloved, having brought under control that Supreme Brahman which transcends the qualities (guṇas), is changeless, and is ever-manifest,
perform the offering unto Brahman.
The gross [aspect], known as one's own action (svakarma), is designated as the oblation; having been grasped by the Supreme, that subtle [aspect] is offered as an oblation by Brahman.
One should perform the removal of karma while remaining as motionless as the fire of Brahman;
one must not depart from the vow of Brahman through absorption in the work of Brahman.
Or rather, O Lord of the Gods, this very thing is proclaimed in the scripture of the Gītā for the sake of Arjuna’s awakening during the great battle at the end of the Dvāpara age.
Indeed, knowledge is offered to Brahman by means of offering to Brahman, and meditation likewise;
devotion, yoga, ritual action, and charity—all are established in the offering to Brahman. (7)

O Queen of the Gods, having abandoned attachment to actions that yield worldly merit, one attains union with the actions of Brahman; it cannot be otherwise, just as [the reflection] in a mirror [is not separate from its cause].
O auspicious lady, this meritorious *brahmarpaṇa* destroys the afflictions of worldly existence,
brings about the destruction of sins, and bestows the fruit of absolute liberation (*kaivalya*).
Among thousands of men, only a few remain established in the offering to Brahman;
those seized by karma do not know that the mind is essentially the nature of action and time.
Therefore, the highest beings should not rely on mental action as the ultimate reality;
rather, they should rely on yoga and virtuous action that is free from mental constructs.
Know this to be the offering to Brahman, and that very act is the sacrifice to Brahman;
knowledge consisting of the realization of Brahman is traditionally known as meditation on Brahman. (12)
Whatever scriptures exist that express synonyms for Brahman, they all originate from Brahman; therefore, one should contemplate Brahman.
O beloved, some say that the self-nature alone is the supreme deity, while others say it is time; some say it is destiny, and others say it is desire.
O you whose nature is consciousness, though abiding in both the moving and the unmoving, you are of the nature of constant awareness;
you are indifferent yet the supervisor, like the wind within the selves of embodied beings. 15.
This Self of beings, the Lord of beings, the creator of beings, being joined with his own power, Māyā, creates, protects, and again dissolves all beings.
Deluded by ignorance, everyone fails to remember the supreme Hari, by whom the universe is set in motion and by whom this world is always protected. (17)
The Self of the gods, the splendor of the world—just as these deities move according to his will, so do we hear his roar; with an excellent form, let us worship that Wind with an oblation. 18.
Thus says the Śruti.
The Yajurveda, beginning with the Ṛgveda, sings of the Supreme Lord;
He is perceptible to all beings, yet though He is seen, He is not grasped.
Though he is perceptible, he becomes imperceptible due to one's own meager fortune—
he by whom even Brahmā and the other gods were sustained through his own creative power (māyā).

One should attain that Hari, who is all-pervading, peaceful, residing within the body, and consisting of pure consciousness, by means of the path of yoga according to the scripture; therefore, one should practice yoga.
Nothing whatsoever taught in the scripture is devoid of yoga;
however, due to the many divergent assertions of teachers, a division within the scriptures is observed. (22)
That yoga which is practiced through all dharmas is most difficult to attain;
that yoga is proclaimed in the Veda as arising from the union of prāṇa and apāna.
The unification of the downward-breath (apāna) and the upward-breath (prāṇa) is remembered as the unsurpassed yoga;
this is the true essence of the scripture, for there is no other means to liberation.
Due to fear of the dissolution of time, Brahmā became devoted to breath control (prāṇāyāma), as did the yogis and sages; therefore, one should restrain the vital breath.
The yogi devoted to *prāṇāyāma* is born equal to Śiva;
for without *prāṇāyāma*, O auspicious one, the practice of yogis is indeed a mockery. (26)

The restraint of the vital breaths (prāṇas) must be performed to sustain the body, the prāṇas, and so forth; through the movement within the internal channels (nāḍīs), there shall be the offering unto Brahman. || 27 ||
Praiseworthy and of meritorious deeds, the sage devoted to breath control (prāṇāyāma) becomes liberated while living; he himself becomes a sky-farer (khecara). || 28 ||
For one who effects the piercing of the six cakras, there shall be the offering unto Brahman;
by the piercing of the six cakras, what deity on earth cannot be mastered? (29)
[Thus ends the sixth chapter in the Śrī Akulāgama Mahātantra, the Yogasārasamuccaya, in the dialogue between Īśvara and Pārvatī. || 6 ||
The Goddess said:
O God of gods, Lord of the universe, Savior from the ocean of worldly existence! O Lord, you have now spoken of the six chakras; what is their essential nature?
By whom was this sixfold [system] composed, and what is the sequence of its divisions?
O Lord of Gods, you should explain it in its entirety, by what means [it was established].
The illustrious Lord said:
And the means for differentiation shall be the first support;
that support is to be known as established in its own activity. (3)
How can one devoid of right conduct possess the intellect for yoga? Therefore, one should at all times abandon that person who performs actions unbecoming to their stage of life (āśrama). || 4 ||
Knowledge devoid of action is destroyed, and action devoid of knowledge is destroyed;
having abandoned both, the agent [of destruction] perishes; therefore, knowing this, one should perform action.
First, purification must be performed; second is that enjoined by the Vedas. Having washed one's feet and sipped water according to the rule, || 6 ||
Having first performed the ritual bath for the washing away of impurities according to the prescribed rules,
he should put on that garment which is free from dirt.
One should apply the *tilaka* on the twelve limbs and hold *darbha* grass in the hands at sunrise; one must never let the time for the twilight (*saṃdhyā*) ritual pass.
Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) first, one should recite the *gāyatrī* mantra one hundred and eight times;
then, according to the occasion, one should perform that which is designated as the "cause and effect" (*kāryakāraṇa*).
The perfection of the dharma of action consists in the contemplation of both action and Brahman;
such knowledge of Brahman and dharma is thus the means for achieving liberation.
The man who, being deluded, attempts to practice yoga by abandoning his prescribed duties, will undoubtedly encounter thousands of obstacles. || 11 ||
But when knowledge is distorted by obstacles, his intellect is produced [in such a way];
by that intellect, one of evil conduct surely falls into hell.

Those who delight in the ritual section (karmakāṇḍa), who are peaceful, free from delusion and envy, and who are wise—O Lord of Yogins, they alone are the upholders of my [teachings], and no others. (13)

The means for accomplishing that karma consists of yoga, as well as listening to the Vedānta, the observance of the Ekādaśī vow, giving gifts according to one's capacity, and the worship of Śiva. (14)
Faith in all dharmas, genuine friendliness, forbearance, compassion, service to sacred fords, purity, non-stealing, and non-acceptance of gifts. || 15 ||
One should practice celibacy, moderation in food, and humility free from pride; one should abandon sleep and laziness, and avoid lust and anger.
Non-violence, truthfulness, freedom from malice, honoring one's mother and father, service to teachers, and kindness toward one's elders and kinsmen—[these are the virtues]. (17)

Freedom from greed regarding the objects of the senses, performance of one's duties, association with the virtuous, and detachment from the objects of the senses—this is the means for achieving yoga. 18.
Through the path of conduct of the virtuous, dispassion arises;
through dispassion, the mind becomes established in yoga that is free from worldly existence. 19.
Thereafter, the attainment of a true guru occurs with certainty through merit;
by whose grace the supreme yoga and knowledge are obtained. (20)
One should not abandon action; rather, one should practice the accumulation of dharma.
Since yoga arises through action, how could one renounce action? (21)
For the sage who desires to ascend to yoga, action is said to be the means;
for that same person once established in yoga, tranquility is said to be the means.
The practice of yoga should be performed in a place free from disturbances, accompanied by the restraints (yamas), the observances (niyamas), and likewise by the performance of virtuous deeds.
In a solitary, secluded, and delightful place, free from fear— in a cave,
in a sacred spot, or even in a temple of the gods— (24).
In a perfected sacred field, at a great pilgrimage site, in the hermitage of the Ancient Puruṣa,
and in a merit-filled place fashioned by the imagination, the perfection of meditation arises.
One should diligently construct a hermitage either in a house or on pure ground;
having perfumed it with excellent incense, one should practice yoga there.
At the beginning of the worship of Gaṇeśa, one should first worship Durgā and Viṣṇu;
having bowed to the lotus feet of the Guru and meditated upon me as Sadāśiva. (27)
Having established within the monastery a very beautiful seat, free from any restriction, gentle, and causing delight to the mind. (28)
Neither too elevated nor too low, the seat of Kuśa grass belonging to the Jina should be spread there; having assumed the Siddhāsana posture upon it, one should hold the body straight. || 29 ||
Having made the body motionless and fixing the gaze between the eyebrows,
one should practice breath control (prāṇāyāma) according to the path instructed by the guru.
One should indeed fill [the breath] through the left channel and hold it again according to one's capacity;
one should exhale through the right and likewise fill it once more.
Having performed the *kumbhaka* as before, one should exhale slowly through the *iḍā*;
by practicing in this manner, the purification of the channels (*nāḍī-śuddhi*) arises. (32)
One attains awakening of the fire element, health, resonance, luster, and lightness;
the retention of the breath as desired is achieved, and the purification of the channels is obtained. (33)
The exertion of one who does not perform the purification of the channels will be in vain;
therefore, the purification of the channels should be performed with every effort. (34)
Having practiced inhalation (prāṇa) upon the lunar part, one should practice exhalation (pāna) upon the solar part;
between the moon and the sun, one should meditate upon the Supreme Lord.
One should contemplate Sadāśiva, the God who resides within the Suṣumnā, situated from the Ādhāra up to the Kula, immovable and devoid of sound, perceivable through meditative realization. || 36 ||
One should meditate upon supreme bliss, free from the duality of existence; through the complete piercing of the six chakras, it is not otherwise within the scope of conceptual meditation. (37)
The apāna-cakra is called the ādhāra, the seat of prāṇa;
samāna is maṇipūra, and udāna is known as anāhata. || 38 ||
The fifth is indeed said to be Vyāna, the supreme and pure Cakra;
and the sixth, situated in the lotus, is declared to be of the nature of space (vyoma). || 39 ||
In this context, Māyā consists of the phonemes and is permeated by the names of the Mothers;
through her, all the cakras within the body are brought into being.
The six wheels arising from the Mātṛkā are those with two petals, sixteen spokes, twelve spokes, ten spokes, six petals, and four [petals]. || 41 ||
She is known as Varṇāvāsāntikā, residing in the center of the apāna-cakra;
O beautiful one, she is the syllables beginning with *va* in the prāṇa-cakra.
The letters beginning with ḍa and ending with pha are said to reside in the Samāna-cakra;
those ending with ka are twelve and are said to reside in the Udāna-cakra.
Those known as the sixteen vowels are situated in the wheel of the vyāna breath;
however, two reside in the wheel of space (vyomacakra), having the nature of the *haṃsa* and the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
The letter *ha* is to be known as the vital breath (*prāṇa*), and the letter *sa* is said to be the downward breath (*apāna*).
The knot of these two, the *prāṇa* and *apāna*, is situated at their entry and exit. (45)
O Goddess, that wheel, existing in the form of the individual soul (jīva) within all bodies, is proclaimed as the six wheels (ṣaṭcakra), by which bondage is produced. || 46 ||
The wheel situated in the apāna, known as the ādhāra and the sun, is pierced by the prāṇa-wheel; the prāṇa-wheel is of the nature of Śiva.
As long as there is a connection with the six chakras, so long is one said to be in saṃsāra;
therefore, by piercing the six chakras, the yogi shall go to the state of Brahman. || 48 ||
Brahman, pervading all vital breaths, is the moment of expansion therein;
the wheel situated in the apāna is the foundation known as Sūrya. 49.
The Svādhiṣṭhāna is proclaimed by the wise; that wheel is gradually differentiated.
In the Samāna [channel], it is joined with the third, for the sake of the fire born of the Samāna. || 50 ||
Where the body is filled by means of the jewel, the thread, and the wind within the wheel of the navel-center, that is called Maṇipūraka.
The knot is pierced by the piercing [force] arising from the udāna;
the wheel called anāhata, which is situated within, is produced by the udāna. || 52 ||
In the pure state, that which is to be pierced does not exist; it is remembered as the pure [state] born of the vyāna wind.
The sixth, indeed, is the wheel of command (ājñācakra), which is declared to be of the nature of space.

By means of that pure wheel, having pierced [the body], he pierces the Command; through the piercing of the six wheels, there is no other means for piercing the wheels than the vital breath (prāṇa). || 54 ||
The foundation (ādhāra) has four petals, while the self-abiding (svādhiṣṭhāna) has six;
the jewel-filling (maṇipūra) has ten spokes, and the unstruck (anāhata) has twelve.
The pure Ājñā-cakra, said to have sixteen [petals], has two petals;
it is one of the six cakras intended for the vital breath (prāṇa), and it is divided by the prāṇa and apāna.
In this way, indeed, by means of breath control (prāṇāyāma), the piercing of the wheels (cakrasaṃbhedya) arises;
for he who possesses the nature of the wheel of vital breath becomes his own piercer. || 57 ||
Even the single wind is the creator through its ten forms, O Lord of the Wind;
the entire wheel of worldly existence arises from the vital breath alone.
Therefore, that restraint of the vital breath (prāṇa) should be performed by men of sattvic nature;
for the vital breath is the all-pervading Brahman, and everything is established within the vital breath. || 59 ||
Know that Prāṇa to be motionless, formless, and stainless;
those who know the Vedas declare it to be absolute liberation, the eternal Brahman. (60)
O Goddess, this secret heart of the Veda-shastra, which is supreme knowledge of Brahman, has been preserved by me in concealment. 61.
Through knowledge of this, there would be no body; from ignorance arises the birth of the body.
This power of karma exists only so long as the [notion of] self persists.
Today I have taught you this non-conceptual knowledge of the Self, which is difficult even for the gods to attain; I should not bestow it upon others.
They were heretics, devoted to sin, nihilists with a lack of discernment, lecherous toward women, of wicked conduct, ungrateful, and hypocritical in their behavior. (64)

Those who have fallen from their duties, those whose pride has been shattered, those who indulge in censure and idle speculation, those who are wrathful, those who are violent, as well as those who are hypocritical and backbiters; || 65 ||
Those who associate with the wicked are dull-witted, insane, and cause suffering to others;
they are greedy for wealth, deceitful in nature, harsh, and fond of quarreling. (66)
One should strictly conceal the knowledge of those who act for their own self-interest, who cause the destruction of the Vedic path, and who are mere logicians and disputants. (67)
That lowest of men who considers even a maiden as his own property—one should know him to be most sinful and should avoid him from afar. (68)
Otherwise, performing actions while established in pride, one does not awaken;
fallen into the flow of the qualities and with wisdom destroyed, one goes downward.
To one who reviles Śiva, reviles yoga, or reviles the scriptures,
the entirety of knowledge should not be given from the perspective of the ultimate truth.
Silence should indeed be observed by those who know reality and are experts in the scriptures;
having ascertained the characteristics of the disciple, one should impart the knowledge of the Self.
"It is my firm conviction that [this] must not be given to an unworthy disciple;
for in the former Satya Yuga, O Goddess, all things were entirely pure. (72)
I have revealed this knowledge for the sake of the liberation of all;
by the power of self-knowledge, a man becomes devoted to the study of the Vedas. (73)
Through practice, having dissolved into the thought-free state along with my body, Time— the life-force of the universe— became directly manifest to me.
With a formless nature, he spoke in a gentle voice:
"And you, by means of your fabricated scriptures, turn people away from me. (75)
"And protect me, so that this creation may proceed ever further";
thus spoke the Supreme Self, and she herself was born as such. (76)
O auspicious lady, this knowledge of Śiva was concealed by me for that reason;
likewise, O beloved, an increase of worldly existence occurs without the knowledge of one's own self.
O Goddess, that supreme and subtle knowledge has now been obtained by you;
he who possesses this knowledge in this world is Śiva himself, assuming a human form.
He who is seen by the disciple as a teacher, yet possesses no supreme knowledge, is indeed a sinner and most base. (79)
He for whom there is the definitive determination of the Self becomes a Guru who severs the bonds.
This Self is supreme, infinite, perceptible, and has the void as its form. (80)
Thus he knows that Hari is the wise one who must be known as the Guru;
for indeed, there is nothing found here in this world as purifying as knowledge.
O Daughter of the Mountain, you must preserve with effort that which is to be kept secret;
it is the very essence of the meaning of the Vedas, the singular unifying conclusion of all the scriptures.
The true nature of reality has been declared, that most secret knowledge of Brahman.
[Thus ends the seventh chapter in the Śrī Akulāgama Mahātantra, in the Yogasārasamuccaya, in the dialogue between Īśvara and Pārvatī. || 7 ||
The illustrious Goddess said:

The entire essence of the meaning of the Vedas, the true state of reality as explained through the single consistent voice of all scriptures, and the knowledge of Brahman that has been well-guarded, has been declared here. (1)
The illustrious Lord said:
All this supreme internal knowledge has been imparted by me;
it is the path of Agni and Soma, characterized by dissolution, and is the heat of the passion for the initiation of Śiva.
Having heard the words of Śambhu, she who possesses the great power of illusion (Māhāmāyā),
filled with joy and struck with wonder, spoke to the eternal Rudra, the one with the eye in his forehead.
The Śrī Devī said:
But I have heard from Māyādevī herself about the unprecedented piercing of the six cakras—
that initiation situated within yoga which even Maheśvara does not know.
You are the preceptor of all the gods and the bestower of fearlessness upon the worlds; O Lord of Gods, be gracious and, O Śaṅkara, explain the initiation.
The illustrious Lord said:
The entire treasury of knowledge is bestowed, and the mire of karma is washed away;
through this conjunction of bestowing and washing, the Self is designated as *dīkṣā*.

Initiation (dīkṣā) should be known as threefold: the individual (āṇavī), that which is called the intellectual (vedhasaṃjñakā), and the third should be known as the divine (śāmbhavī); thus the division is declared to be threefold.
The first initiation belongs to Ānavī; it consists of a single mantra and two syllables.
It is renowned as "Short" within Brahman, and it is established by the mantra itself.
The second is known by the name Dīrghasaṃjñā, remembered as Vedhavatī;
it consists of two mātrās joined with three, and possesses three mātrās conjoined with four.
It is flooded, immortal, secret, accessible through knowledge, and the nectar of the waters;
it is perfectly fashioned by means of the *praṇava*—the gross, the subtle, and the supreme.
The threefold initiation, consisting of tradition and scripture, resides within one's own body;
the reality awakened above is known as Śiva-nature below.
That initiation is declared to be the *āṇavī*, situated within the first *praṇava*;
by it, one's own nature, which was previously agitated by *kuṇḍalinī*, is well-pierced upward. (12)
That initiation is known as *vedha* (piercing) when performed in the second *praṇava*;
its pervasiveness extends upward, and by that, it is well-pierced above.
And she is renowned as Śāmbhavī within the third, which consists of the Praṇava;
Brahmā is established in the first, and Viṣṇu indeed in the second.
The third form, that of Śiva, should be known by the wise;
it is the one reality that has become threefold, acting as the cause of creation, preservation, and destruction. (15)
Though it is evident to all beings, those of wicked intellect do not know it:
that the *recaka* is the awakening of Śāmbhavī, and the *kumbhaka* is conjoined with Śakti.
The *āṇavī* [piercing] is to be known as the *pūraka* [inhalation], resting upon the mind and the vital breath;
the piercing by means of mantra (*mantravedha*), the piercing by means of power (*śaktivedha*), and the piercing of Śambhu (*śāmbhavī vedha*) are thus described. (17)
Initiation has been described as threefold; now listen to its characteristics.
When facing westward, the subtle mind arises within the liṅga. (18)
That initiation, well-expounded through mantras, is called *āṇavī*;
by that [initiation], the mind is bound to the sign (liṅga) adorned with fire.
Then, through that piercing, it certainly becomes known as "possessing penetration" (vedhavatī);
liberated from the three qualities, the mind shall become upward-moving.
Through the movement within the inner channel, one should attain dissolution into the Liṅga of Space;
then that is the Śāmbhavī initiation—one should know it as the cutter of the net.
