All sages pierce [the centers] through the various methods of breath control (prāṇāyāma).
Thus has initiation been described by me as having three forms, born of one's own nature.
Those who know what is beneficial are blessed teachers upon this earth;
know that others are deceivers, devoted only to their genitals and bellies.
Those whose minds are permeated by ignorance do not regard the initiation of yoga as being outside of ritual action; such is the understanding held by those possessed by nescience. (24)
They proclaim to one another the existence of reality within unreality;
O Goddess, through the gaze of the Guru, piercing occurs within the disciple. (25)
Fainted and fallen upon the ground, she thought, "This is that initiation which liberates from bondage," and by her power of action, she moved about with the movements of a monkey.
Knowledge is far removed from them; O beloved, how could there be the initiation of Brahman?
That initiation which exists within sacrificial mantras does not bestow liberation in this way.
Initiation indeed arises from the Praṇava; through it, one removes what has been accumulated [by past karma].
Mantras and yantras are the descent of power (śaktipāta); that initiation does not occur otherwise.
Deluded by ignorance, the world proceeds through false conduct;
they do not find the Śāmbhavī initiation, nor likewise the Āṇavī piercing.
Established in the initiation of yoga through the pride of vain conduct,
they repeatedly deceive themselves whom they have already deceived.
The teachers, together with their disciples, descend [into the lower realms], of this there is no doubt;
the Kaulas do not understand the Kula, nor the instrument, nor likewise the cause.
Deprived of self-knowledge, they honor initiation in a contrary manner;
with minds delighted by sense objects, they consider the body to be the self.
Like madmen they chatter, never remembering Sadāśiva;
though he is before their very eyes, they do not recognize him, deluded by my māyā.
Those who take refuge in me alone cross over this illusion;
through association with the virtuous, they shall indeed possess the Kaulika initiation and knowledge.
By means of which the most terrible suffering born of saṃsāra is destroyed—that supreme spiritual initiation (dīkṣā) must indeed be obtained through the compassion of the Guru. (35)
That which abides in its own intrinsic nature is considered supreme bliss;
there is no merit equal to initiation, and there is no austerity equal to initiation.
There is no meditation equal to initiation; therefore, one should take refuge in initiation.
That which is indeed yoga is initiation—that is what has been described by me as initiation.
And it has been declared by Akulanātha that the Akula is devoid of Kula.
[Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Exposition of Initiation," in the Śrī Akulāgama Mahātantra, the Yogasārasamuccaya, within the dialogue between Īśvara and Pārvatī. || 8 ||
Oṃ, homage to Brahmā.
The illustrious Goddess said:
O Lord, formerly there were four stages of life (āśramas) for those belonging to the Vāyavya hermitage; there was no fixed sequence among them, yet their spiritual realization was clearly perceived.
The student, the householder, the forest-dweller, and likewise the ascetic—tell me, O Lord of the Śūras, how one attains from one stage of life (āśrama) to the next. || 2 ||
O Mahādeva, their ultimate state is brought about by that very action;
tell me, O Śaṅkara, what else is external within the application of that action? (3)

What is the nature of the student life (brahmacarya) for those who have entered the first stage of life today? And what is the second, the householder's life, and the third, the forest-dweller's life? || 4 ||
And the fourth stage of life, O Śambhu, is proclaimed as renunciation (saṃnyāsa).
[Its practitioners are] the Haṃsa, the Paramahaṃsa, the Triḍaṇḍī, and the Daṇḍadhṛk.
Abiding in the dharma of renunciation, what is the nature of the Great Saying (mahāvākya)?
What is its inquiry like, by which liberation is produced? (6)
O Lord, O Maheśvara, show me mercy; tell me truly, what kind of destiny awaits one whose religious merit has been rendered fruitless by the duties of the four stages of life?
Regarding the attainment of the formless from the formed, what is the nature of their worship?
O Sadāśiva, tell me here of his essential nature, both with attributes and eternally without attributes.
What is the nature of the Prāṇaliṅga taught by Śiva in the scripture?
O Lord, what else consisting of Brahman has been proclaimed?
"This word is well-known in the world; however, one should wear the *prāṇaliṅga*.
O Bull-bannered One, what kind of wearing (*dhāraṇā*) is that? Please explain. (10)
In which places and with which flowers should one worship the Prāṇaliṅga? Who possesses the authority among the castes, what is the mantra, and for whom is the worship intended? (11)
O Mahādeva, Lord of the World, grant the answer to these very questions—[an answer] that is all-knowing, true, and a liberator from ignorance. (12)
O Lord of the World, you are the worthy refuge; you are the purifier of the impurities of the mind.
O lamp of knowledge, the destroyer of the darkness of ignorance, salutations to you!
Protect me, O Śaṅkara, Lord of Beings; I have fallen into the ocean of worldly existence.
You ought to sever this unbearable suffering of dwelling in a womb.
My mind has always been bewildered by the contradictions of endless scriptures;
O Lord, grant me certainty and tell me the means of liberation. (15)
The illustrious Lord said:
The fourfold order of society was created by me according to the division of qualities and actions;
know me to be its creator as well, yet the immutable non-doer.
Within the four-fold caste system, three castes are the twice-born;
likewise, there are the four Vedic castes and the stages of life (āśramas). || 17 ||
The student, the householder, the forest-dweller, and likewise the ascetic—let them proceed from stage to stage of life, following the eternal dharma of the stages. (18)
Thinking thus, O Queen of the Gods, those established in worldly toil do not know the supreme Dharma by which liberation is produced. (19)
O Goddess, one who has attained the worldly stages of life is indeed recognized as an ascetic; since you abide in the stage of virtue, how could you ever reach a state devoid of qualities? 20.
Through the external stages of life, the fruit of heaven is obtained exactly as enjoined by the rules;
however, if the rites are omitted in a stage of life, the one belonging to that stage shall go to hell.
The entire world is extroverted and functions through external objects; therefore, by whatever intellect this [world] is perceived, all beings are deluded by it. 22.
O beloved, those who believe that liberation is attained through external efforts and separate religious duties certainly deceive themselves by the latent impressions of their karma. (23)

O Goddess, those who have reached perfection in yogic practices through the integration of the four stages of life (āśramas) are called "internal laborers" (antaraṅga-śramas) within the scriptures. 24.
Listen to the description of the meritorious and divine hermitages known as the Adhyātma;
situated in the midst of Tāraka, they are proclaimed to be established in satisfaction.
The first is Maṇipūra, the second is Anāhata, the third is Nirañjana, and the fourth is Nirālaya. || 26 ||

The student (brahmacārī) resides in the [first] jewel; the householder (gṛhī) is in the second stage of life (āśrama); the forest-dweller (vānaprastha) is the third; and the ascetic (yati) is said to be the fourth. || 27 ||
I abide in all stages of life; I am the bearer of the triple staff and the wielder of the staff.
Those who rely on external appearances of the stages of life have resorted to false ego.
The student (brahmacārī) has the restraint of speech, the initiated (dikṣita) has the restraint of mind,
the forest-dweller (vānaprastha) has the restraint of action, and the ascetic (yati) should possess the restraint of knowledge.
The staff of speech, the staff of mind, and the staff of action—these are the three;
he by whom these staffs are restrained is established as a bearer of the triple-staff (tridaṇḍin).
Wearing the topknot, the sacred thread, and so forth, clad in ochre robes, and carrying the triple staff—
he should perform whatever external rites are prescribed even while established in actionlessness (naiṣkarmya).
One should renounce the topknot, the sacred thread, and so forth, as well as the triple staff;
wearing ochre robes and holding the staff of knowledge, one should practice the state of absolute actionlessness alone.
The triple-staff is the supreme staff; the staff of knowledge is ever-arisen.
By that staff, the renunciant is celebrated as "the single-staffer. (33)
He whose crest consists of knowledge, unlike the other crests of fire, is called a wise man who possesses the true crest; others are merely wearers of a sheath.
This Sūtra is the state of Brahman; for one whose consciousness consists of its retention, by virtue of retaining that Sūtra, he shall be neither impure from food remnants nor unclean.
They say that what is not a Sūtra is a Sūtra, for the name "Sūtra" is handed down through tradition;
by that [name], all this is proclaimed as a Sūtra, like clusters of jewels on a string.
He in whose body the form of Brahman, which is bliss, is established, moves about in the state of Brahman; he is called a *brahmacārī*. 37.
Even though the *praṇava* is unmanifest, he who sacrifices by offering the clarified butter of contentment as fuel and slaying the senses as the sacrificial animals— he alone is truly initiated.
Having a triangular shape like a blazing fire, with the flame of fire burning in its center, he who stands in the midst of the forest of Kandarpa is called a forest-dweller (vānaprastha). || 39 ||

Having attained the fourth stage of life (turyāśrama), one who bears three staffs (tridaṇḍī) or a single staff (ekadaṇḍadhṛk) is designated as a Haṃsa; he who has heard all [the Vedas] is known as a Parahaṃsa. || 40 ||
Having meditated, "I am that Brahman—consciousness free from all limiting adjuncts and untainted"—how could one still belong to a caste or stage of life? || 41 ||
The Haṃsa who abides in the system of castes and stages of life is praised as the Parahaṃsa;
the Parahaṃsa possesses firm knowledge, is self-reliant, and is free from the fever of worldly passion.
The swan, measuring sixteen finger-breadths, moves externally;
it does not rest due to its flickering nature as it flows through the left and right channels.
When the haṃsa alone is the constant supervisor, and the mind is perfectly motionless above it, then that parahaṃsa remains as duality; at that time, he becomes absorbed in That.
Otherwise, due to the difference in physical form or the distinctions of caste and stage of life, their state as the *haṃsa* or the *parāhaṃsa* is not observed within the scriptures. (45)
The *haṃsa* is devoid of the three qualities (*triguṇa*); this is the sequence [of stages] known as *parahaṃsa*.
Since there is no perception of the *haṃsa*, how could there be a *parahaṃsa*? (46)
Renunciation is declared to be the giver of liberation through the inquiry into the Great Sayings (mahāvākya);
by means of the Great Yoga and the Great Saying, it is proclaimed by those who contemplate reality.
That statement by which the renunciant is fully described is indeed the form of the *haṃsa*, abiding within all beings. (48)
But how can there be an inquiry into the Great Sayings (mahāvākya) merely through the recitation of the scriptures?
I shall now explain the meaning of the term "inquiry into the Great Sayings."

This Great Saying (mahāvākya), which has been proclaimed here, is not to be uttered; it is the consciousness of all things yet devoid of specific consciousness, abiding within various other statements.
By the word "vi," the stainless movement of the *haṃsa* (the Swan) established therein is indicated;
this is the investigation of the Great Saying (*mahāvākya*) situated within the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas. (51)
Those who have realized the Great Saying (mahāvākya) through service at the feet of the Guru are indeed declared to be renunciants (saṃnyāsins); others are merely bearers of the name.

O Goddess, this well-spoken [treatise] on the characteristics of renunciation, which is entirely in accordance with the body, has been declared by Hari to Arjuna according to the prescribed rule. (53)
The wise understand *saṃnyāsa* to be the renunciation of optional rites;
the discerning declare that *tyāga* is the relinquishment of the fruits of all actions. (54)
Some wise men have declared that action should be abandoned as being full of defects;
others, however, have said that action consisting of sacrifice, charity, and austerity should not be abandoned. 55.
Thus spoke the Lord Viṣṇu, the noble-minded one, to Dhanañjaya:
"Of these, there is but one that is agreed upon; only the names appear to be different. (56)
Others [assert] an abundance of conceptual constructions imagined through various doctrines; yet, O auspicious lady, there is no separate doctrine within the Vedas or in all the scriptures. (57)
Listen to all that, O auspicious lady, which will be for your welfare;
I shall describe to you correctly the dharma characterized by renunciation.
The wise know the renunciation of optional rites as *saṃnyāsa*;
they call those [rites] "optional" by which the body is obtained. (59)
Rajas, sattva, and tamas—these qualities born of Prakṛti are the causes of creation, maintenance, and destruction; they belong to the Great Sovereign.
O highly fortunate lady, for them renunciation is said to be achieved through action;
this is indeed the supreme renunciation, but now hear the opinion of others. (61)
The wise declare that the renunciation of all actions is the renunciation of offerings;
that mental action which is passionate (rājasa) or ignorant (tāmasa) is said to be [false renunciation].
The quality of *sattva*, consisting of *rajas* and *tamas*, is declared to be the nature of the fruit;
having abandoned that fruit by means of the path of Brahman, such renunciation is proclaimed.
"O Goddess, some wise men say that action should be abandoned as being full of fault, while others declare it must be performed; this was well-determined by Hari for both Arjuna and you."
"O beloved, the threefold mental action should not be abandoned even if it possesses faults;
likewise, others say that the actions of sacrifice, charity, and austerity should not be abandoned. (65)
I shall relate to them everything that is in their minds according to the truth:
regarding the entry into the sacrificial rite, the practice of breath-retention (kuṃbhaka), and the act of giving.
Know that austerity and ritual action belong to the third [world], which is entirely free from affliction.
O beloved, all this, beginning with rites for specific desires, has been declared by me.
Among all stages of life, the student (brahmacārī) is praised for his pure body;
so too are the Sūdadohas verses and those who have been consecrated (dīkṣitāḥ).
The forest-dweller (vānaprastha) is Sūdadohas; he should chant the Sūdadohas verse.
Likewise, the student (brahmacārī) is in the ten-spoked [wheel], and the householder (gṛhī) is in the twelve-spoked [wheel]. (69)

In the sixteen-spoked [cakra] of the forest-dweller (vānaprastha), the ascetic (yati) is said to reside in the two petals; for him there is no stage of life (āśrama) pertaining to the body, as he becomes one whose stage of life is the *sūdadohas* verse.
Therefore, the staff and the ochre robe are useless for one who dwells in an external stage of life;
even he who abides in all stages of life [is not liberated] by means of his own ritual actions and mental activities.
Wherever and in whatever manner one's karma dictates, there and in that manner one should act;
know this, O Pārvatī, as the well-known *sūdadohas* verse in the Ṛgveda. (72)
He is considered the conscious one (cetas), the intelligent one (cit), the self-dependent one (svātman); he is regarded as the heart (hṛdaya) and the mind (mānasa).
He is known as the person (puruṣa), the swan (haṃsa), the knower of the field (kṣetrajña), and the sustainer of the body (dehadhāraka). || 73 ||
Indeed, in all the scriptures, this great one is proclaimed as the Inner Controller (Antaryāmī), the Sūdadohas, the Supreme Brahman, the Supreme Self, and Hari himself. (74)
This self-established one, who is within as light, is devoid of qualities (nirguṇa) and the driver of the machine;
yet that Lord, by means of Māyā, has entered various wombs in his own essential form.
By the designation of "above" and "below," he is called a transmigrating being (saṃsārī);
though devoid of qualities (nirguṇa), he is subject to the qualities (guṇādhīna) and, through Māyā, becomes the cause of creation.
The notion of being a "living soul" (jīva) arises for him as he exists within his own bodies;
yet, through practice, even though he possesses qualities, he becomes transcendent of those qualities.
The Supreme Brahman is to be known by oneself; what purpose, then, do the stages of life (āśramas) serve?
For one who is disciplined, renunciation of action is indeed attained. (78)
The abandonment of that [knowledge] through delusion is proclaimed to be of the nature of darkness (tāmasa).
Therefore, by means of the yoga of support, the *sūdadohas* verse is praised. (79)
Through practice, the entire fruit of the stages of life (āśrama) is attained, and not otherwise;
some who know reality, having resorted to the dharma of renunciation (saṃnyāsa), understand this.

When, through the correct retention of yoga, one abides in the conventional sign established within one's own self, and by piercing the knot in the heart, one becomes transcendent of the qualities (guṇas). || 81 ||
Then he becomes a *paramahaṃsa*, a *tridaṇḍin*, and a bearer of the single staff (*ekadaṇḍadhṛk*);
by wearing the ochre garment and carrying the staff, he is a true renunciant (*saṃnyāsī*). (82)
One who merely bears the name is not called a Haṃsa, nor a Parahaṃsa;
liberation is not found in external signs, for it is remembered that internal [realization] alone bestows liberation.
In the worship of external symbols, the bearer of the symbol may be one who carries three staffs or one who carries a single staff;
indeed, a person becomes a "tridaṇḍin" (bearer of the triple-staff) through the restraint of speech, mind, and action.

A yogi should carry the triple staff (tridaṇḍa) with his body, but not the Vaiṣṇava staff; that bamboo staff is for the sake of livelihood, whereas the triple staff is the means for liberation from the body. || 85 ||
Therefore, having abandoned the triple staff and all those means for performing ritual acts, the ascetic,
devoted to yoga, should wander with unmanifested signs.
One should always wear the Vaiṣṇava mark for the sake of receiving hospitality, honor, and worship;
he should not be called a renunciant (saṃnyāsī), for a true renunciant is one who is devoted to yoga.
And when the attainment of vision occurs, then there is no doubt that one is a haṃsa;
as a true haṃsa of Sadāśiva, one has forgotten both knowledge and the object of knowledge.
O Goddess, without the yoga of the Self, how can one become a celibate student (brahmacārī), or indeed a householder, a forest-dweller, or an ascetic? For none of these exists without yoga.
For men who take pride in ritual action, what fruit indeed can there be from an āśrama?
Liberation is the fruit of the āśrama; it is not attained through ritual action. (90)
Liberation is attained through action; this is declared in all the scriptures.
Indeed, yogis worship that very action as the nature of the Self.
The karma that binds one to saṃsāra, such as sacrifices, gifts, and the like—
even if it be free from obstacles— will nevertheless continue to yield its fruit.
Devoid of knowledge, these beasts believe that falsehood is not false;
they think clearly that the fruit of action must be experienced by Brahmā and the others who performed it. 93.
Action that inevitably yields fruit destroys the yoga of one's own self;
by such action, the branches of the tree of saṃsāra flourish. (94)

Those of dull intellect believe that action appropriate to one's caste and stage of life, when conjoined with the renunciation of its fruits, is what leads to liberation; thus they engage in such acts out of devotion.
Some are proud of their ritual actions, some are proud of their devotion;
some are proud of their scriptures, and some are proud of their sacred fords.
Therein, some have pride in the ego; some have pride in the field (kṣetra);
some have pride in the elements (bhūta); and some have pride in names. || 97 ||
Some take pride in mantras, some take pride in meditation;
some take pride in austerity, and some take pride in charity.
Seized by arrogance, they remain established on the path of karma;
they do not know the way of yoga, by which the perfected ones have gone to Śiva.
In the first part of the Veda, the section on ritual action (karmakāṇḍa) is proclaimed;
it consists of both engagement and renunciation, and is beneficial as it possesses duality. (100)

The body exists through the function of the qualities (guṇas), and within the body, suffering is most intense; therefore, all this is suffering, and it is the opinion of the wise that karma must be abandoned. 101.
In this most terrible cycle of existence, due to base qualities such as sin and the like,
people do not remember the supreme reality, for ignorance is exceedingly powerful.
The workings of diverse karma are difficult to overcome even for the gods;
having abandoned yoga, men become engaged in other dharmas. (103)
People perform actions for the sake of happiness, yet happiness is not found through action, O beloved; those mortals who are bereft of destiny do not find the means to happiness.
O sinless one, [the world] is born through the activity of creation, maintenance, and destruction;
yet creation, maintenance, and destruction cease through the yoga of knowledge.
All yogis know their own yoga, which is the abode of bliss, wherein one is indeed firmly absorbed in Brahman without effort. (106)
That evil-minded man who treats yoga with contempt is of wicked conduct and most sinful; he shall go to hell after his death. || 107 ||
He whose mind, even when directed toward yoga, proceeds from a sinful disposition due to fate, is a righteous soul of meritorious fame and is honored by gods and men. (108)

O Daughter of the Mountain, who can truly comprehend the greatness of one established in yoga—how he attains the state of union, the source of all perfections, while an unperfected man [attains only] the abode of the gods? 109.
In this matter, know that there is consensus regarding the auspiciousness of the Gītā scripture;
listen with faith, O Goddess, for I shall speak to you in brief. (110)
Having attained the worlds earned by merit and having dwelt there for countless years, he who has fallen from yoga is born again in the house of the pure and the prosperous.
Or else, one is born into a family of wise yogis;
for such a birth as this is indeed difficult to obtain in the world. (112)
There he regains that very same mental disposition belonging to his former body;
from that point on, O joy of the Kurus, he strives even further toward perfection.
Having heard these words of Kṛṣṇa, O son of Pāṇḍu, Vībhatsu,
whose mind was then firmly fixed on yoga, praised the god Nārāyaṇa.
O Dear One, for one who attains non-conceptualization through meditation and other means, there is liberation without a doubt; he attains union [with the Divine]. 115.
The Great Goddess Maheśvarī, who increases knowledge, should be known as the practitioner of the rite by means of which the yogi is sustained within her own womb. 116.
The latent impressions of karma are most powerful and difficult to conquer in this world of saṃsāra;
he by whom they have been conquered in this world is considered a blessed man. (117)
Having obtained a human birth, which is so difficult to attain, if one does not awaken to the supreme knowledge of Nirvana, that man should contemplate his own true nature. 118.
Moreover, what is the use of much speaking here? Listen, O long-eyed one:
the fruit of all stages of life resides within the heart of that yoga.
He is praiseworthy, virtuous, blessed, and the glory of his lineage; he is wise and should be known as a righteous-souled sage devoted to the practice of yoga. || 120 ||
Even those Brahmins who are devoted to the six duties, who are most righteous householders, they too attain liberation; this is proclaimed from the midst of the Vedas.
The best among the knowers of reality has described that action as being of six kinds:
performing sacrifices, officiating at sacrifices, merit, and likewise the study of the Purāṇas. (122)
Teaching, giving, and receiving—which takes the form of merit—constitute the practice of the six duties; liberation is truth, and that I shall now declare to you. (123)
Sacrificing is said to be in the *ādhāra*; officiating at sacrifices (*yājana*) is in the *svādhiṣṭhāna*; studying is in the *maṇipūra*; and teaching is in the *anāhata*. (124)
O Goddess, beloved, this giving at the wheel of purification and receiving at the wheel of command is certain for the sake of liberation from karma. 125.
O bound one, the cause of liberation is seen through the Vedic scriptures;
by that [contrary] action, the destruction of the intellect arises for human beings. (126)
Having abandoned this activity known as phenomenal expansion (prapañca), one should practice yoga;
[this applies to] Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, others, women, and so forth. (127)
There is no distinction of caste here; this eternal dharma of yoga is to be practiced by all castes and stages of life as the everlasting Brahman.
Through association with them, the intellect is born for the practices of hearing about the inner self and so forth;
and herein, association with the virtuous is declared to be the first means.
Through merit, the company of the virtuous is attained for the sake of yoga;
indeed, for men fallen into the cycle of worldly existence, the company of the good is truly beneficial.
From association arises yoga, which cuts through the snare of illusion;
therefore, those who desire liberation should cultivate association with the virtuous.

Having abandoned the supreme Dharma through one's own effort, one should not resort to another Dharma; for what wise man, having abandoned the nectar of immortality, would wander about as a beggar, O dull-witted one? (132)
Without the knowledge of Brahman, there is no unbroken happiness in the world;
that knowledge of Brahman which brings about liberation is obtained from the mouth of the Guru. (133)
Thus, O Goddess, this which has been well-ascertained by me has been revealed to you;
it was concealed in all the tantras for the sake of expanding the ritual applications. 134.
Those mounted on the chariot of great yoga proceed along the path of Brahman;
whereas those mounted on the chariot of karma go into the ocean of worldly existence.
Through prior reflection, an action performed with its constituent qualities is traditionally held to grant heaven;
however, if that same action is devoid of those qualities, it leads to hell.
Indeed, by means of yoga, for the perfected ones there is no rebirth even if [the practice] is inverted;
if one should fall from yoga, one will attain the station of Brahmā and the other gods.
In this world, the practice of ritual action is difficult to accomplish and brings the suffering of rebirth;
whereas, O beloved, the practice of yoga is truly easy and bestows happiness. (138)
Those men who are averse to yoga should be known as unfortunate;
Mahāmāyā, who is the body of Hari, has not been propitiated by them, she who is Kuṇḍalinī.
He whose mind is set upon yoga is the most excellent among all people;
even he who has rejected yoga should be known as the lowest. (140)
O Goddess of the gods, those mortals who revile the path of yoga are of wicked conduct, even though they may appear to abide in virtuous behavior.
Good conduct is the first dharma; Acyuta is the lord of dharma.
O Goddess, he is attained through the practice of yoga, and not otherwise. 142.
Now, therefore, I shall fully declare what the fruit is and what the destination;
for those in the stages of life (āśramas), yoga is the fruit, and liberation is recorded as their destination. (143)

For those who, having honored the attainment of the formless through the formed, still seek further excellence—how can there be the attainment of yoga for them, whose minds are shrouded by ignorance? (144)
He who, out of delusion, abandons me—the Self and the Lord dwelling within all beings—and worships my image instead, he merely offers oblations into ashes. (145)
I am the self of all beings, eternally abiding within all beings;
yet, disregarding me, that mortal brings about his own humiliation. (146)
I am indeed the self of all beings and the creator of beings;
O friend, the Brahman of sound and the Supreme Brahman are my eternal body.
The Self is spread throughout the world, and the world is situated within the Self;
both are pervaded by Me, and both are established in Me.
That by which the formless is attained is that which is embodied and situated within the body;
it is that by which the physical frame, appearing as the qualities of all the senses, moves.
That which is conjoined with all external qualities is sung as the Sound-Brahman (Śabdabrahman); those who are well-versed in its forms proceed to the Supreme Brahman and beyond. 150.
Know that worship performed toward an image bestows rewards within this worldly existence;
indeed, liberation is not attained through it even in hundreds of millions of births. (151)
Otherwise, they perform actions in one way and desire the fruit in another;
O Goddess praised by heroes, how can there be liberation through the act of creation? (152)
He who plants a neem tree for the sake of mango fruit should be known as one of dull intellect; his mental aspiration will be fruitless.
Likewise, they do not worship the image at all, nor do they desire eternal fruit;
deluded by Māyā, they do not know the essence of essences. || 154 ||
Sadāśiva, who exists within the physical body, is to be worshipped with the flowers of inner disposition;
he alone is indeed the Puruṣa, the Self, who assumes his true nature while abiding within Prakṛti. (155)
The Lord himself is established as the fourfold collection of beings;
though infinite and abiding in all states, he is likewise proclaimed to possess attributes.
All this—the past, the future, and that which is present—is indeed the Puruṣa alone;
by him this entire universe is pervaded, and he stands transcending it by the measure of a span.
From its own locus, this vital breath falls away and heats the exterior;
thus, having departed from the Virāj, the person (puruṣa) becomes like a grain of rice.
The embryo of all the creators of the universe, possessing the power of divine action and the self,
divided himself by himself into one way, ten ways, and three ways.

For the Supreme Self is indeed the single portion of the self belonging to all beings without exception; that which is manifested today as an incarnation is not perceived as distinct from the aggregate of living beings.
"Accomplish the self, accomplish the god, and accomplish the being"—thus it is threefold;
the Virāj is with the presence, and the vital breath is unified by means of the heart. (161)
That embodied one, when thus remembered, should be understood by those seeking liberation;
his worship must be performed with unwavering control of the prāṇa and apāna breaths.
One should worship the threefold human flower before Śrī Śiva. O beloved, all this regarding the worship of the Saguna [Brahman] has been told to you. 163.
Whether a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, a Śūdra, or those of other castes, those who desire the supreme reality must perform the worship of Śiva. (164)
That worship of the God of gods which consists in accordance with his qualities, in that way one obtains the divine fruit of liberation; of this there is no doubt. || 165 ||
O beloved, external worship should not be performed, for it creates obstacles to liberation;
therefore, the Infinite One, who is higher than the highest, should be worshipped with the three qualities.
That worship of the Supreme Lord is called "unsupported" (nirālambā);
it should be performed through breath control (prāṇāyāma) according to the characteristics of Kula-yoga. 167.
That worship consisting of sixteen services which is prescribed for the image does not yield the fruit of liberation; this must be understood by those who desire liberation. (168)
One who considers external objects to be certain, eternal, comparable, and worthy of worship—by whom they are deemed eternal—is a fool among men, like an elephant. (169)
This has been correctly explained to you; now listen to the *prāṇaliṅga*.
One should meditate upon the *prāṇaliṅga*, which is declared to have the form of the Moon. (170)
Fools who imagine themselves to be wise do not understand the meaning of the name; how can a fabricated, perishable symbol (liṅga) become the liṅga of the vital breath? || 171 ||
They consider the Prāṇaliṅga, the excellent Lord, to be within their own bodies;
but how could those whose minds are shrouded by ignorance perceive the Jñānaliṅga? 172.
The Prāṇaliṅga is formless, all-pervading, facing every direction, perceptible, omnipresent, and pure; it is seen, yet it cannot be grasped as an object. || 173 ||
When the Śaiva scripture has been expounded, what kind of meditation (dhāraṇā) is that which consists of being marked by the prāṇaliṅga? O Bull-bannered One, let it be told. (174)
The *prāṇaliṅga*, which consists of dissolution, is to be known within the interval between day and night;
through its retention, the resonance situated at the *dvādaśānta* is to be realized. (175)
First, one should hold [the breath] at the navel and worship it with the flowers of contemplation;
likewise, O fair-faced one, at the heart, the throat, and the middle of the eyebrows. (176)
Above that, O Goddess, one should hold the immovable and imperishable sattva;
at the end of the twelve [finger-breadths], one should worship the prāṇaliṅga with the flower of the individual soul (jīva). || 177 ||
Indeed, Aghora is not prescribed for the worship of the Prāṇaliṅga;
having performed one hundred thousand or one hundred thousand repetitions [of the mantra], one should perform the worship. || 178 ||
A hundred is indeed the form of Brahmā, a thousand is that of Viṣṇu, and a hundred thousand is said to be the intermediate [form] of Śiva; all these are of the nature of the vowels.
In this very manner, the recitation of one hundred thousand [times] is taught in the treatises on inner yoga as that which is designated as a "lakh" (one million) for the sake of liberation. 180.

The distinction between short, long, and protracted [vowels] corresponds to two, three, and four corners [of the phonetic grid]. Recitation (japa) is traditionally held to consist of one, two, and three measures (mātrās) respectively. || 181 ||
The wise should understand that each subsequent stage is indeed superior:
the number [of repetitions] for the worshiper is one hundred, and likewise one thousand for the practice of breath-retention (kuṃbhaka).
The count of one hundred thousand for the exhalation (recaka) is achieved by repeating [the mantra] three times;
thus, the recitation performed within the body is remembered as that which brings about the destruction of both sin and merit.
This constant practice of the *praṇava* is said to be for ascetics; this method of recitation in yoga, which is non-terrible (*aghora*), has been described by me. (184)
In the worship of the Prāṇaliṅga, indeed no other mantra is proclaimed than that which those who know Brahman in this world recognize as the supreme Śiva.
In their propitiation, direct perception does not clearly occur;
rather, in the Kṛta, Tretā, and Dvāpara ages, many [attain results] simply by meditating with the mind.
Others, devoted to the conduct of the learned, are knowers of Brahman even once in the Kali age;
for a knower of Brahman is rare in the world and remains established in a concealed form. || 187 ||
Through divine vision born of meritorious deeds, he beholds that [state] which has been attained in this human birth, arising from knowledge and realization. (188)
He who does not delight in the self shall never attain security;
but he by whom the self is fully known is proclaimed here as the true teacher.
O auspicious lady, how can one established in the state of a guru do so without self-knowledge, when he must seek within the body the ever-arisen Linga of one's own Self? (190)
He is Maheśvara, he is the perfected soul, he is the ascetic and the yogi, he is indeed the Vaiṣṇava; he is the celibate student, the initiated, the forest-dweller, and the true ascetic. || 191 ||
She too should be known as a sage whose soul is fixed on Dharma and who delights in the practice of Yoga;
that which is the duty of the social classes and stages of life has been described by me as Sadharma (the True Dharma). || 192 ||
It is taught that there is no other dharma that constitutes liberation apart from breath control (prāṇāyāma);
devotion, beloved austerity, charity, initiation, and the cessation of inhalation [are its components]. (193)
When all vital breath is rendered non-slaughterable, the *praṇava* is said to be yoga;
the yogin who is supreme in *prāṇāyāma* is also Viṣṇu and Maheśvara.
The yogi embodies all the gods; therefore, one should not show him contempt.
Contempt for one engaged in yoga causes the destruction of one's lifespan and merit. 195.
His consort, of beautiful limbs, bestows the fruit of all desires;
through the practice of yoga, the yogi becomes possessed of infinite majesty. (196)
Indeed, that yoga which has the form of nectar is called "Kinnara" for living beings; through the practice of yoga, one becomes both with form and without form, though possessing a body. (197)
For this supreme yoga of Śiva and the individual soul arises from practice;
that yoga of Śiva and the individual soul does not depend on the doctrines of various teachers.
But within the inner science (adhyātmaśāstra), O fair-faced one, there is no difference;
it is spoken of in many ways, O beloved, for the purpose of expanding the treatise. 199.
Therefore, various types of yoga have been devised by living beings;
the secret of all yoga is what is accepted by diverse philosophical systems. (200)
Indeed, all the determinations of yoga exist within the Akula-āgama; O beloved, this which is to be strictly guarded has been told by me to you in this scripture. 201.
There are many paths regarding action, but for Yoga there is no fixed rule;
diversity is seen in Yoga through action in the form of illusion (māyā).
For the cutting away of that action, knowledge is the supreme preeminence of one's own Self. 202.
In the scripture on destruction, a distinction is conceived by all [schools] apart from self-knowledge;
that which is well-known as the "path of the young" (kumāramārga) is this determination of breath-control (prāṇasaṃyama). || 203 ||
Truth, truth, and again truth—this very truth has been spoken by me:
there is no other path to yoga, O sinless one, than through the vital breath (māruta).
The supreme secret of the knowledge of Brahman has been set forth in this scripture, as well as its equivalence to the Vedic scriptures, for the sake of uplifting the world. (205)
For that deity who is indeed the Lord of the Unfamily (Akulanātha), whose nature is equanimity, and who is accompanied by Sā (?
and Vāhuka (?), this scripture was not composed by him because it is beyond the reach of the Unfamily (Akula). || 206 ||
In the past, I propitiated that immutable one through breath control;
the Great Viṣṇu of the first kalpa appeared before my very eyes.
At that time, O Goddess, by the grace of the Supreme Brahman, I heard this entire great scripture, which reveals the depths of the Vedas.
That which was to be obtained later has been performed by him through his own *māyā* for the sake of creation;
that scripture is now proclaimed—keep it secret, O Maheśvarī! (209)
O beloved, my command should be remembered: knowledge must be imparted even to those men who are wicked in conduct and full of deceit. (210)
The illustrious Goddess said:
The duration of the Kali age will be four hundred and forty years; at that time, Maheśvara [will appear].
O Lord, O Master, out of compassion for living beings in this most terrible Kali age, which is full of untruth and suffering, please spread forth knowledge.
On the southern side of the Vindhya mountains, on the southern bank of the Gaṅgā,
I shall there relate this family tradition in the form of a brahmin.
In the Kali age, the knowledge of the manifold Self will arise for the sake of upholding the truth and for the delusion of the wicked. 214.
O one of great austerity, this which is to come has been told by me today;
for the greatness of knowledge in the Veda is indeed immeasurable and beyond the scope of the senses.
O Lord of the Gods, he perceives the Lord of All together with the Bindu situated in the midst of the Nāda,
located within the Kula at the navel, heart, throat, and the end of the play of the eyebrows.

By means of breath control (prāṇāyāma) through the sequence of purifying the channels (nāḍī-śuddhi), the practitioner becomes a yogi; he is renowned as one who is liberated while living (jīvanmukta). || 217 ||
But that liberation which occurs at the fall of the body is not true liberation, O beloved;
for without breath control (prāṇāyāma), O auspicious lady, the body will simply fall away.
Therefore, those who desire liberation must practice the restraint of the vital breath (prāṇa);
there is no other path for that which is approved by all the scriptures. (219)
Know that this path has been taught with its underlying rationale;
it is the very essence of the Akula-āgama—take this to heart. (220)
O Great Goddess, remember my words clearly again and again:
one should dwell within the *kula* by means of the middle path of internal restraint.
But he who, O auspicious lady, considers knowledge superior within the Akulāgama, as taught by the Lord of Akula—he is Akula, devoid of Kula. (222)
The Lord, who pervades all bodies everywhere like space, has composed this scripture which brings about the severance of bondage. || 223 ||
This must not be disclosed and must be strictly concealed from those whose minds are afflicted by sin;
it should never be spoken to anyone at all, but only to those who are endowed with righteousness. 224.

The internal states would be the ultimate, like gold because of their stainlessness; for those who are already pure, there is no further purification, O best of knowers of Brahman, due to their stainlessness. (225)
There is no dharma higher than yoga; there is no austerity higher than yoga;
there is no meditation higher than yoga; there is no happiness higher than yoga. || 226 ||
O fair-faced one, that man is blessed whose mind is fixed on yoga;
he should be known as the destroyer of worldly existence, having his destiny within the lineage of Māruta.
One should practice breath control (prāṇāyāma) precisely according to the sequence beginning with the postures;
through such practice, the vital breath spontaneously ascends to the sphere of space (vyomamaṇḍala).
O fair-faced one, this yoga is to be understood from all the scriptures;
indeed, the secret of the Akula tradition is to be known through the grace of the Guru. (229)

whether it be correct or incorrect, let no fault be attributed to me.
